q: A competitive inhibitor with K<sub>i</sub> = 5 µM is present at 10 µM. Without inhibitor, the enzyme's K<sub>m</sub> is 2.0 mM. What is the apparent K<sub>m</sub>?
e: Apparent K<sub>m</sub> = K<sub>m</sub>(1 + [I]/K<sub>i</sub>).
1 + 10/5 = 3, so apparent K<sub>m</sub> = 2.0 × 3 = 6.0 mM (V<sub>max</sub> unchanged).

q: A drug binds an enzyme's active site and competes with the substrate. How does it affect Km and Vmax?
e: A competitive inhibitor competes for the active site.
More substrate is needed to reach half of Vmax, so the apparent Km increases.
At very high [S], substrate outcompetes the inhibitor, so Vmax is unchanged.
t: Competitive = 'can be outcompeted' = same Vmax. On a Lineweaver–Burk plot the lines cross on the y-axis.

q: Alcohol dehydrogenase converts ethanol and NAD⁺ into acetaldehyde and NADH. To which enzyme class does it belong?
e: Ethanol is oxidized while NAD⁺ is reduced.
Enzymes that catalyze redox reactions (dehydrogenases, oxidases, reductases) are oxidoreductases.

q: An enzyme's activity vs. pH is bell-shaped: it rises steeply around pH 4 and falls steeply around pH 6.5. Mutation studies point to an aspartate and a histidine in the active site. Which model fits best?
o: Asp must be ionized (COO⁻) and His must carry its extra H⁺
Asp must be protonated (COOH) and His must be neutral
Both groups must be neutral for the enzyme to work
Both groups must carry a positive charge to work
e: The rise near pH 4 matches Asp losing its H⁺; activity needs COO⁻.
The fall near 6.5 matches His losing its H⁺; activity needs protonated His. Only between the two pK<sub>a</sub>s are both forms correct, giving the bell shape.

q: An enzyme follows Michaelis–Menten kinetics. At [S] = 3Km, what fraction of Vmax is the reaction rate?
e: v = Vmax[S] ÷ (Km + [S])
= Vmax(3Km) ÷ (Km + 3Km) = 3/4 Vmax

q: Two substrates compete for the same enzyme. Substrate A: k<sub>cat</sub> = 100 s⁻¹, K<sub>m</sub> = 0.1 mM. Substrate B: k<sub>cat</sub> = 400 s⁻¹, K<sub>m</sub> = 2 mM. Both are present at the same low concentration. Which is converted faster?
o: A, about 5 times faster than B
B, about 4 times faster than A
B, about 20 times faster than A
Both are converted at equal rates
e: When substrates compete, the ratio of rates equals the ratio of k<sub>cat</sub>/K<sub>m</sub> × [S].
A: 100/0.1 = 1000 mM⁻¹ s⁻¹. B: 400/2 = 200 mM⁻¹ s⁻¹. Equal [S], so A is 1000/200 = 5 times faster.

q: What does an enzyme’s Km represent in Michaelis–Menten kinetics?
e: At [S] = Km, v = Vmax/2 for Michaelis–Menten behavior.

q: On a Lineweaver–Burk (double-reciprocal) plot, the y-intercept equals:
e: 1/v = (Km/Vmax)(1/[S]) + 1/Vmax
y-intercept = 1/Vmax; x-intercept = −1/Km; slope = Km/Vmax.

q: With substrate in large excess and all other conditions constant, the total enzyme concentration is doubled. What happens?
o: V<sub>max</sub> is unchanged; K<sub>m</sub> is halved
e: V<sub>max</sub> = k<sub>cat</sub>[E]<sub>T</sub>, so doubling [E]<sub>T</sub> doubles V<sub>max</sub>.
K<sub>m</sub> is a property of each enzyme molecule and its substrate, so it stays the same.

q: An allosteric activator binds an enzyme that shows sigmoidal kinetics. How does the rate vs. [S] curve change?
o: It shifts left: less substrate gives half-maximal rate
It shifts right: more substrate gives half-maximal rate
It becomes linear, with no saturation at high [S]
It is unchanged, since activators only alter V<sub>max</sub>
e: Activators stabilize the high-affinity (R) state.
Substrate binds more easily, so the curve moves left (lower K<sub>0.5</sub>) and becomes less sigmoidal.

q: Many active sites use a histidine side chain as a general acid–base catalyst. Why is histidine well suited to this role?
o: Its pK<sub>a</sub> (≈ 6) lets it gain or lose H⁺ near pH 7
Its side chain is a strong acid that is always ionized
Its side chain stays positively charged at any pH
Its aromatic ring stores electrons for redox steps
e: Near physiological pH, significant amounts of both the protonated and neutral forms exist.
So histidine can donate a proton in one step and accept one in another.

q: At 37 °C (where 2.303RT ≈ 5.9 kJ mol⁻¹), an enzyme lowers a reaction's activation energy by about 18 kJ mol⁻¹. Assuming the Arrhenius pre-factor is unchanged, by roughly what factor does the rate increase?
e: k ∝ 10<sup>−E<sub>a</sub>/(2.303RT)</sup>, so the rate ratio is 10<sup>ΔE<sub>a</sub>/(2.303RT)</sup>.
18/5.9 ≈ 3, so the rate increases by about 10³ = 1000-fold.
t: Each ~6 kJ mol⁻¹ off E<sub>a</sub> at body temperature ≈ 10× faster.

q: A single-chain protein contains about 150 amino acids. Using an average residue mass of 110 Da, what is its approximate mass?
t: Quick estimate: kDa ≈ number of residues × 0.11.

q: A disulfide bond forms between two:
e: Two –SH groups are oxidized to form –S–S– (cystine).
Reducing agents like β-mercaptoethanol break disulfides.

q: Poly-L-lysine is a random coil at pH 7 but folds into an α-helix at pH 12. What best explains this?
o: Deprotonated side chains no longer repel each other
High pH forms disulfide bonds that brace the helix
High pH hydrolyzes peptide bonds into short helices
Side chains form salt bridges with each other at pH 12
e: Lysine's side chain pK<sub>a</sub> is about 10.5, so at pH 7 every residue is –NH₃⁺ and the like charges push each other apart.
At pH 12 the side chains are neutral –NH₂, so backbone H-bonds can hold an α-helix.
t: Like charges packed along one chain push it apart; neutralize them and helices can form.

q: A histidine side chain (pK<sub>a</sub> = 6.0) is on a protein in a solution at pH 7.0. About what fraction of these side chains is protonated (positively charged)?
e: Henderson–Hasselbalch: pH − pK<sub>a</sub> = 1, so [neutral]/[protonated] = 10¹ = 10.
Protonated fraction = 1/(10 + 1) ≈ 0.09, or about 9%.

q: Which two standard amino acids have side chains that end in an amide group (–CONH₂)?
e: Asparagine (Asn) and glutamine (Gln) carry –CONH₂ on their side chains.
Aspartate and glutamate have –COO⁻ instead; they are the acidic 'parents' of Asn and Gln.
t: Asn/Gln = 'amide twins' of Asp/Glu: swap –O⁻ for –NH₂.

q: Two amino acids join to form a dipeptide. Which statement is correct?
o: It is a hydrolysis reaction that consumes water
It is a condensation reaction that releases water
e: The −COOH of one amino acid reacts with the −NH₂ of the other.
An −OH and an −H leave together as H₂O (condensation, or dehydration).
The new C–N bond is a peptide (amide) bond.
t: Building polymers releases water; breaking them (hydrolysis) uses water.

q: Histidine has pK<sub>a</sub> values of 1.8 (α-COOH), 6.0 (side chain) and 9.2 (α-NH₃⁺). What is its isoelectric point?
e: List charges: below 1.8 the net charge is +2; 1.8–6.0 it is +1; 6.0–9.2 it is 0; above 9.2 it is −1.
The neutral form exists between pK<sub>a</sub> 6.0 and 9.2, so pI = (6.0 + 9.2)/2 = 7.6.
t: Average the two pK<sub>a</sub>s on either side of the neutral (net 0) form.

q: In collagen, every third residue is glycine. Replacing one of these glycines (as in some forms of brittle bone disease) weakens the triple helix. Why?
o: Only glycine's tiny side chain fits in the crowded helix center
Glycine forms the disulfides that link the three chains
Glycine is the residue that vitamin C–dependent enzymes hydroxylate
Glycine's charged side chain repels water from the helix
e: In the triple helix, every third residue faces the packed center where the three chains meet.
Only glycine (side chain = H) fits there; any larger side chain pushes the strands apart.

q: A researcher unfolds an enzyme with urea and β-mercaptoethanol, then slowly removes both. The enzyme refolds and becomes fully active again. What does this show?
o: The primary sequence contains all the information needed for folding
Chaperones must be present for the protein to refold correctly
Disulfide bonds, not the sequence, dictate the folded structure
Urea and β-mercaptoethanol never fully denatured the enzyme
e: Removing the denaturants let the chain refold on its own into its active shape.
So the primary sequence alone determines the 3D structure (Anfinsen's classic experiment).
t: Real cells use chaperones to prevent misfolding and aggregation, but the folding information is in the sequence.

q: Amino acids in human proteins have which configuration at the α-carbon?
o: A racemic mix of D and L
e: Proteins in humans are built almost entirely from L-amino acids.
Most are (S) by the Cahn–Ingold–Prelog system; cysteine is the (R) exception.

q: The α-helix and β-sheet are stabilized mainly by:
o: Hydrogen bonds between backbone C=O and N–H groups
e: Secondary structure = local folding of the backbone.
It is held together by hydrogen bonds between backbone carbonyl O and amide H atoms.
R-group interactions (disulfide, ionic, hydrophobic) mainly drive tertiary structure.
t: Secondary = backbone H-bonds. Tertiary = R-group interactions.

q: What is the net charge of free glutamate at pH 7.4?
e: α-COO⁻: −1. Side-chain COO⁻: −1 (pKa ≈ 4.1). α-NH₃⁺: +1 (pKa ≈ 9.5).

q: A 10-base-pair DNA segment contains 4 G–C pairs and 6 A–T pairs. How many hydrogen bonds hold its two strands together?
e: G–C pairs have 3 hydrogen bonds; A–T pairs have 2.
4 × 3 + 6 × 2 = 12 + 12 = 24 hydrogen bonds.

q: In DNA, guanine pairs with cytosine using how many hydrogen bonds?
e: G–C: 3 hydrogen bonds. A–T: 2 hydrogen bonds.

q: The antibiotic ciprofloxacin inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase, a topoisomerase. Why does this stop bacterial DNA replication?
o: Supercoiling builds up ahead of the fork, so the DNA can't be unwound further
Okazaki fragments can no longer be joined into one continuous lagging strand
RNA primers are no longer removed from newly made DNA
Mismatches can no longer be proofread during replication
e: Unwinding at the fork overwinds the DNA ahead of it.
Gyrase normally removes that strain; without it, tension builds until helicase and the fork stall.

q: Why do linear chromosomes lose a little DNA from their ends with each round of replication if telomerase is absent?
o: The last RNA primer on the lagging strand can't be replaced with DNA
Leading-strand synthesis cannot begin at the chromosome's origin
Helicase cannot unwind the final few thousand base pairs
Ligase removes the terminal nucleotides after each round
e: After the RNA primer at the very end of the lagging strand is removed, there is no upstream 3′-OH for polymerase to extend into the gap.
That end stays short, so each round trims the chromosome (the end-replication problem).

q: A nucleotide consists of:
o: A phosphate group, a five-carbon sugar and a nitrogenous base
A five-carbon sugar and a nitrogenous base, with no phosphate
A phosphate group, a six-carbon sugar and a nitrogenous base
A phosphate group, an amino acid and a nitrogenous base
e: Nucleoside = sugar + base. Nucleotide = nucleoside + phosphate(s).

q: The two strands of a DNA double helix are:
o: Joined by covalent bonds between bases
e: The strands run in opposite directions.
That's why replication needs a leading and a lagging strand.

q: A virus's DNA genome is 25% A, 33% T, 24% G and 18% C. What is the best conclusion?
o: The genome is rich in G–C base pairs
e: In double-stranded DNA, A = T and G = C (Chargaff's rules).
Here A (25%) ≠ T (33%) and G (24%) ≠ C (18%), so the bases are not paired: the genome is single-stranded. It contains T, so it is DNA.
t: Chargaff's rules hold only for double-stranded DNA. A ≠ T is the giveaway for single strands.

q: Which DNA molecule would have the highest melting temperature (Tm)?
e: G–C pairs have 3 hydrogen bonds and stack more strongly.
More G–C content means more energy is needed to separate the strands.

q: Starting from one double-stranded DNA molecule, about how many copies exist after 10 PCR cycles (ideal efficiency)?
e: Each cycle doubles the DNA: 2¹⁰ = 1024 ≈ 1000.
20 cycles gives about a million.

q: Which technique detects a specific DNA sequence?
e: Southern = DNA; Northern = RNA; Western = protein. ELISA uses antibodies to detect proteins or antigens.

q: Which enzyme makes the short RNA primers that DNA polymerase extends during replication?
e: DNA polymerase cannot start a chain from scratch; it needs a free 3′-OH.
Primase lays down short RNA primers that supply that 3′-OH.

q: Which enzyme seals the gaps between Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand?
e: Ligase forms the final phosphodiester bond between fragments.
Helicase unwinds, primase makes RNA primers, topoisomerase relieves supercoiling.

q: In sickle cell disease, a β-globin codon changes from GAG (glutamate) to GUG (valine). This is a:
e: One base is substituted (A → U in the mRNA), so the reading frame is unchanged.
The new codon specifies a different amino acid (Glu → Val), which is a missense mutation.
t: Missense = Mis-matched amino acid; nonsense = stop; silent = same amino acid.

q: Which enzyme attaches the correct amino acid to its tRNA?
e: Each synthetase recognizes one amino acid and its tRNAs, using ATP to 'charge' the tRNA.
This step is the real decoding step that makes the genetic code work.

q: An E. coli strain has a lacI mutation that makes a nonfunctional repressor. When grown with no lactose and no glucose, its lac genes are:
o: Transcribed at a high level anyway
Silent, because no inducer is present
Transcribed only after lactose is added
e: With no working repressor, nothing blocks the operator, so expression no longer requires lactose (constitutive).
With glucose absent, cAMP–CAP is bound, so transcription is high.
t: Broken repressor (lacI⁻) = always on. CAP still needs low glucose for high-level transcription.

q: In E. coli, glucose is low and lactose is present. What is the status of the lac operon?
o: Repressor released; CAP–cAMP bound; transcription high
Repressor released; CAP unbound; transcription off
e: Lactose (as allolactose) binds the repressor and releases it from the operator.
Low glucose raises cAMP, which binds CAP; CAP–cAMP helps RNA polymerase bind the promoter.
Both conditions together give high transcription.
t: The cell's logic: 'I'm out of my favorite sugar (glucose) and lactose is here, so make lactose enzymes.'

q: In bacteria, ribosomes can begin translating an mRNA before its transcription is finished, but this does not happen in human cells. Why?
o: Human transcription occurs in the nucleus, and translation in the cytoplasm
Human ribosomes can bind only the 3′ end of an mRNA
Bacterial mRNAs are made 3′→5′, so the start codon leaves the polymerase last
Human mRNAs have no start codon until they are spliced
e: Bacteria have no nucleus, so a new mRNA's 5′ end is exposed to ribosomes while RNA polymerase is still working.
In eukaryotes, pre-mRNA is capped, spliced and exported from the nucleus before ribosomes can reach it.

q: During elongation, a new aminoacyl-tRNA enters the ribosome at the:
e: A (aminoacyl) site: new tRNA arrives. P (peptidyl) site: holds the growing chain. E (exit) site: empty tRNA leaves.
Order of movement: A → P → E.

q: Why can one tRNA often read more than one codon for the same amino acid?
o: Pairing at the codon's third position is flexible ('wobble')
Pairing at the codon's first position is flexible
Adjacent codons overlap, sharing bases with each other
Ribosomes edit the mRNA to match the tRNA's anticodon
e: The first two codon bases pair strictly; the third allows non-standard pairs (for example G–U).
Wobble also explains why many third-position mutations are silent.

q: Researchers charge a tRNA<sup>Cys</sup> with cysteine, then chemically convert the attached cysteine into alanine. When used in translation, where does this alanine end up in the protein?
o: At positions coded by cysteine codons
At positions coded by alanine codons
At random positions throughout the protein
Nowhere, because the ribosome rejects it
e: The ribosome checks only codon–anticodon pairing, not the attached amino acid.
This tRNA still carries the Cys anticodon, so alanine is placed at Cys codons. Translation accuracy depends on aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases charging tRNAs correctly.

q: In eukaryotes, which RNA polymerase transcribes protein-coding genes into mRNA?
e: Pol I: most rRNA. Pol II: mRNA (and some small RNAs). Pol III: tRNA and 5S rRNA.

q: One nucleotide is inserted near the start of a gene's coding region. What is the most likely result?
o: A frameshift altering all downstream codons, usually yielding a nonfunctional protein
A single amino acid substitution, with the rest of the protein unchanged
No change in the protein, because the genetic code is degenerate
One extra amino acid is added, but the rest of the protein is normal
e: Codons are read in groups of 3 from a fixed starting point.
Adding 1 base shifts every following codon and often creates an early stop codon.

q: A tRNA has the anticodon 5′-IGC-3′, where I is inosine at the wobble position. Which codons can it read?
e: Pairing is antiparallel: anticodon C (3′ end) pairs with codon G (first base); G pairs with C (second base). So the codon is 5′-GC_-3′.
Inosine, at the anticodon's 5′ end, pairs with U, C or A in the codon's third position: GCU, GCC, GCA (all alanine).

q: Translation starts at the first AUG in the mRNA 5′-CCAUGGCUUGAACG-3′. How many amino acids are in the peptide? (UGA is a stop codon.)
e: The first AUG begins at nucleotide 3: AUG | GCU | UGA.
AUG (Met) and GCU (Ala) are translated; UGA stops, so the peptide has 2 amino acids.

q: Liver metabolizes fructose through fructokinase and aldolase B to trioses. Why can large fructose loads drive fat synthesis faster than equal glucose loads?
o: Fructose enters glycolysis below PFK-1, bypassing its main control step
Fructose is phosphorylated by hexokinase, which is never regulated at all
Fructose is converted directly into acetyl-CoA in the liver cytosol
Fructose activates PFK-1 much more strongly than glucose does
e: Fructokinase makes fructose-1-phosphate; aldolase B splits it into DHAP and glyceraldehyde (then phosphorylated to G3P).
These trioses enter after the PFK-1 step, so ATP and citrate can't throttle the flow.
Unchecked triose flux yields excess pyruvate and acetyl-CoA, which the fed liver turns into fatty acids.

q: During a fast, glycerol released from adipose triglycerides is used by the liver for gluconeogenesis. At which intermediate does its carbon enter?
e: Liver glycerol kinase makes glycerol-3-phosphate.
Glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase oxidizes it to dihydroxyacetone phosphate (DHAP), a glycolytic/gluconeogenic triose.
Two trioses then combine via aldolase toward glucose.
t: Adipose tissue has little glycerol kinase, so glycerol travels to the liver to be used.

q: Which enzyme is the main control point of glycogen synthesis?
e: Glycogen synthase adds UDP-glucose units with α(1→4) bonds.
Insulin activates it (by dephosphorylation).

q: In the Cori cycle, lactate from exercising muscle is:
o: Carried to the liver and converted back to glucose
Burned directly by the muscle for ATP
Converted into fatty acids in muscle
e: Muscle makes lactate during intense exercise.
The liver uses it for gluconeogenesis and sends glucose back to the muscle.

q: Which enzyme is the rate-limiting step of the pentose phosphate pathway?
e: G6PD catalyzes the first, irreversible, NADPH-producing step.

q: In the fed state, liver fructose-2,6-bisphosphate levels are high. What is the effect?
o: Glycolysis is stimulated and gluconeogenesis is inhibited
Gluconeogenesis is stimulated and glycolysis is inhibited
e: F-2,6-BP activates PFK-1 (glycolysis) and inhibits fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase (gluconeogenesis).
Insulin raises F-2,6-BP; glucagon lowers it.

q: What are the two main products of the pentose phosphate pathway?
e: The oxidative phase makes NADPH (for fatty acid synthesis and antioxidant defense).
The non-oxidative phase makes ribose-5-phosphate for nucleotides.

q: What is the net ATP produced by glycolysis per molecule of glucose?
e: Investment phase uses 2 ATP.
Payoff phase makes 4 ATP (plus 2 NADH).
Net = 4 − 2 = 2 ATP
t: Glycolysis happens in the cytosol and needs no O₂.

q: How does glucokinase in the liver differ from hexokinase in most other tissues?
o: Glucokinase has a high Km and is not inhibited by glucose-6-phosphate
Glucokinase has a low Km and is strongly inhibited by glucose-6-phosphate
Glucokinase has a high Km and is strongly inhibited by glucose-6-phosphate
Glucokinase has a low Km and is not inhibited by glucose-6-phosphate
e: A high Km means glucokinase works fast only when blood glucose is high (after a meal).
This lets the liver take up extra glucose without stealing it from other tissues during fasting.

q: During glycogen breakdown, which enzyme removes the α(1→6) branch points?
e: Glycogen phosphorylase only cleaves α(1→4) bonds and stops a few residues from a branch.
Debranching enzyme moves the short chain onto another branch and then hydrolyzes the α(1→6) bond, releasing free glucose.

q: Why can't humans make net glucose from even-chain fatty acids?
o: Their product, acetyl-CoA, can't be converted to pyruvate or net oxaloacetate
Their β-oxidation occurs in the cytosol, away from gluconeogenic enzymes
The liver lacks the enzymes needed to oxidize fatty acids to acetyl-CoA
Their acetyl-CoA is entirely consumed making ketone bodies in the liver
e: Pyruvate dehydrogenase is irreversible.
For each acetyl-CoA (2 C) that enters the citric acid cycle, 2 carbons leave as CO₂, so there's no net gain of oxaloacetate.
(Glycerol and odd-chain fatty acids CAN contribute to glucose.)

q: In anaerobic conditions, why do muscle cells convert pyruvate to lactate?
o: To regenerate NAD⁺ so glycolysis can continue
To make extra ATP directly from pyruvate
To regenerate NADH for the electron transport chain
To make glucose in the muscle by gluconeogenesis
e: Glycolysis needs NAD⁺ for the GAPDH step.
Without O₂, NADH can't be reoxidized by the ETC, so lactate dehydrogenase uses NADH to reduce pyruvate, regenerating NAD⁺.

q: Which pair of signals activates isocitrate dehydrogenase?
e: ADP signals that the cell needs energy; Ca²⁺ signals muscle contraction.
ATP and NADH, signs of plenty, inhibit the enzyme, slowing the cycle when energy is high.

q: About how much ATP does complete aerobic oxidation of one glucose produce, using modern estimates?
e: Glycolysis: 2 ATP + 2 NADH. PDH: 2 NADH. Citric acid cycle (×2): 6 NADH, 2 FADH₂, 2 GTP.
Total ≈ 30–32 ATP, depending on which shuttle moves cytosolic NADH into the mitochondria.
Older textbooks say 36–38.

q: Oligomycin blocks ATP synthase's proton channel. Why does electron transport soon slow down too?
o: The proton gradient builds up until pumping H⁺ becomes too hard
Oligomycin also binds and directly inhibits complex IV
The proton gradient collapses, leaving the pumps nothing to work against
NADH can no longer be made, so complex I runs out of substrate
e: With no H⁺ flowing back through ATP synthase, the gradient gets steeper.
Eventually complexes can't pump against it, so electron flow slows (respiratory control).

q: The mammalian ATP synthase c-ring has 8 c subunits. Each full rotation moves 8 H⁺ through F₀ and makes 3 ATP in F₁. About how many H⁺ pass through the synthase per ATP made?
e: Each c subunit carries one H⁺ per turn: 8 H⁺ per rotation.
F₁ has three catalytic β subunits: 3 ATP per rotation.
8 ÷ 3 ≈ 2.7 H⁺ per ATP; adding about 1 H⁺ for importing Pi and exchanging ADP/ATP gives the ~4 H⁺ per ATP used for P/O ratios.

q: How many CO₂ molecules are produced per acetyl-CoA during one citric acid cycle turn?
e: Each acetyl-CoA leads to two decarboxylations in one cycle turn.

q: Electrons from cytosolic NADH that enter through the glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle yield about:
e: This shuttle passes electrons to FAD, which enters at coenzyme Q (skipping Complex I).
So they yield about as much as FADH₂. The malate–aspartate shuttle preserves about 2.5.

q: Which enzyme is the main rate-limiting step of the citric acid cycle?
e: Isocitrate dehydrogenase is activated by ADP and inhibited by ATP and NADH.

q: During muscle contraction, cytosolic Ca²⁺ rises and some enters the mitochondria. How does this affect the citric acid cycle?
o: It activates PDH phosphatase, isocitrate DH and α-ketoglutarate DH
It inhibits PDH phosphatase, isocitrate DH and α-ketoglutarate DH
It activates citrate synthase but inhibits succinate dehydrogenase
It activates PDH kinase, which shuts off pyruvate dehydrogenase
e: Ca²⁺ is a 'contraction is happening' signal, so ATP demand is about to rise.
It stimulates PDH phosphatase (turning PDH on) and directly activates isocitrate dehydrogenase and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, speeding NADH production.

q: Using about 2.5 ATP per NADH and 1.5 ATP per FADH₂, about how much ATP comes from oxidizing one acetyl-CoA in the citric acid cycle and ETC?
e: 1 GTP = 1. Total ≈ 10 ATP

q: No citric acid cycle reaction uses O₂, yet the cycle stops within seconds when O₂ runs out. Why?
o: Without O₂, NADH isn't reoxidized, so NAD⁺ and FAD run out
O₂ is a required allosteric activator of citrate synthase
Without O₂, acetyl-CoA is converted straight into lactate
O₂ is needed to regenerate oxaloacetate directly from malate
e: Four cycle dehydrogenases need NAD⁺ or FAD as electron acceptors.
Only the electron transport chain, ending at O₂, turns NADH and FADH₂ back into NAD⁺ and FAD.
No O₂ → carriers stay reduced → the dehydrogenases stall → the cycle stops.

q: Which molecule carries electrons from Complexes I and II to Complex III?
e: Ubiquinone is a lipid-soluble carrier in the inner membrane.
Cytochrome c carries electrons from Complex III to Complex IV.

q: Isolated mitochondria are given succinate and Pi, and O₂ use is slow. Adding ADP makes O₂ use jump; it slows again once the ADP has been converted to ATP. What does this show?
o: Electron transport is tightly coupled to ATP synthesis
ADP is the final electron acceptor of the chain
Succinate can't be oxidized until ADP activates Complex II
ADP uncouples mitochondria and lets protons leak in
e: Without ADP, ATP synthase is idle, the proton gradient grows, and pumping (and thus electron flow) is opposed.
ADP lets H⁺ flow through ATP synthase, lowering the gradient, so electrons and O₂ use speed up.
This 'respiratory control' means mitochondria burn fuel only as fast as ATP is needed.

q: Beta-oxidation of an even-chain fatty acid primarily yields which two-carbon product?
e: Each beta-oxidation cycle typically removes a two-carbon acetyl-CoA unit.

q: An essential amino acid is one that:
o: Must come from the diet because the body can't make it
Is present in every protein that the body makes
Is made only by the liver and then exported to tissues
Is used mainly as fuel rather than to build proteins
e: Humans can't synthesize 9 amino acids, including leucine, lysine and phenylalanine.

q: Fatty acid synthesis needs acetyl-CoA in the cytosol, but acetyl-CoA is made in mitochondria. How does it get out?
o: It joins oxaloacetate to form citrate, which is exported and cleaved in the cytosol
It diffuses directly through the inner mitochondrial membrane into the cytosol
It is converted to malonyl-CoA, which is then exported to the cytosol
It is converted back to pyruvate, which is exported and then reconverted
e: The inner membrane is impermeable to acetyl-CoA.
Citrate leaves, and ATP-citrate lyase regenerates acetyl-CoA in the cytosol (the citrate shuttle).

q: Using 2.5 ATP per NADH, 1.5 per FADH₂ and 10 per acetyl-CoA, and subtracting 2 ATP equivalents for activation, how much net ATP comes from fully oxidizing myristate (14:0)?
e: 14 carbons → 7 acetyl-CoA after 6 rounds; each round gives 1 NADH and 1 FADH₂.
Minus 2 for activation: 94 − 2 = 92 ATP.
t: Rounds = (carbons ÷ 2) − 1. The last round makes two acetyl-CoA.

q: Which lipoprotein carries dietary triglycerides from the intestine to tissues?
e: Chylomicrons: dietary fat from the intestine. VLDL: fat made by the liver. LDL: cholesterol delivery. HDL: cholesterol return to the liver.

q: The liver makes ketone bodies but can't use them for energy. Why?
o: The liver lacks thiophorase, which converts acetoacetate to acetoacetyl-CoA
Ketone bodies can't cross liver cell membranes to reach the mitochondria
The liver lacks HMG-CoA synthase, which is needed to oxidize ketone bodies
Ketone bodies inhibit β-oxidation, so the liver avoids burning them
e: Using ketones requires succinyl-CoA:acetoacetate CoA transferase.
The liver lacks it, so it exports ketones for other tissues to use.

q: Making one palmitate (16:0) from 8 acetyl-CoA requires how many NADPH?
e: One acetyl-CoA primes the chain; 7 are converted to malonyl-CoA and added, so there are 7 elongation cycles.
Each cycle has two reductions (keto → alcohol, then C=C → C–C), each using one NADPH.
7 × 2 = 14 NADPH.

q: A patient starts a statin. Besides lowering cholesterol synthesis, why does the drug lower blood LDL so effectively?
o: Lower liver cholesterol triggers more LDL receptors, which pull LDL out of the blood
Statins bind LDL particles in the blood and break them down directly
Statins block cholesterol absorption by the intestine, which lowers LDL
Statins convert circulating LDL into HDL, which the liver then clears
e: Liver cells sense their own cholesterol falling.
They make more LDL receptors (through SREBP signaling), clearing more LDL from the blood.

q: Both ketogenesis and cholesterol synthesis in the liver use HMG-CoA. How are the two pathways kept separate?
o: Ketogenesis uses mitochondrial HMG-CoA; cholesterol uses cytosolic HMG-CoA
Ketogenesis uses cytosolic HMG-CoA; cholesterol uses mitochondrial HMG-CoA
Both share one HMG-CoA pool, split by insulin-regulated transporters
Only ketogenesis makes HMG-CoA; cholesterol starts from mevalonate
e: In mitochondria, HMG-CoA synthase and HMG-CoA lyase turn HMG-CoA into acetoacetate (ketone bodies).
In the cytosol, a separate HMG-CoA synthase makes HMG-CoA that HMG-CoA reductase (on the ER) reduces to mevalonate, toward cholesterol.
Mevalonate itself comes from HMG-CoA.
t: Lyase → ketones (mitochondria). Reductase → cholesterol (cytosol/ER).

q: Which enzyme is the rate-limiting step of the urea cycle?
e: CPS I combines NH₄⁺, HCO₃⁻ and 2 ATP into carbamoyl phosphate in the mitochondria.
It requires N-acetylglutamate as an activator.

q: Chronic heavy drinking often causes fatty liver. Ethanol oxidation raises the liver's NADH:NAD⁺ ratio. How does this promote triglyceride buildup?
o: β-Oxidation slows, and more DHAP is reduced to glycerol-3-phosphate
β-Oxidation speeds up, flooding the liver cells with free fatty acids
NADH directly activates lipoprotein lipase on liver cells
Ethanol molecules are linked straight into triglycerides
e: β-Oxidation needs NAD⁺; when NADH is high, fatty acids aren't burned and are re-esterified.
High NADH also drives DHAP → glycerol-3-phosphate, supplying the backbone for triglycerides.
Fatty acids + glycerol-3-phosphate → triglycerides that accumulate in liver cells.

q: How many rounds of β-oxidation are needed to break palmitic acid (16:0) completely into acetyl-CoA?
e: 16 carbons ÷ 2 = 8 acetyl-CoA.
The last round splits a 4-carbon unit into two acetyl-CoA, so only 7 rounds are needed (n/2 − 1).

q: Liver cells and pancreatic β-cells take up glucose through GLUT2, whose K<sub>m</sub> (about 15 mM) is well above normal blood glucose. Why does this suit their job?
o: Their glucose uptake rises in step with blood glucose, so they can sense it
Their glucose uptake stays at its maximum rate even when blood glucose is low
A high K<sub>m</sub> lets them pump glucose against its gradient
A high K<sub>m</sub> keeps glucose from ever leaving these cells
e: When [S] is well below K<sub>m</sub>, the transport rate is roughly proportional to [S].
So GLUT2 cells take up more glucose only when blood glucose is high, letting the liver store excess and β-cells release insulin in proportion.

q: GLUT1 behaves like an enzyme with K<sub>m</sub> ≈ 1 mM for glucose. At a blood glucose of 4 mM, about what fraction of its maximum rate is it working?
e: Rate/V<sub>max</sub> = [S]/(K<sub>m</sub> + [S]).
= 4/(1 + 4) = 0.80, so about 80% of V<sub>max</sub>.

q: Red blood cells (about 0.3 osmol L⁻¹ inside) are placed in either 0.3 M sucrose or 0.3 M urea. What happens?
o: They stay normal in sucrose but swell and burst in urea
They burst in sucrose but stay normal in urea
They stay normal in both, since both are 0.3 M
They shrink in both, since both solutes pull water out
e: Both solutions have the same osmolarity as the cell, but tonicity depends on whether the solute can enter.
Sucrose can't cross, so it is isotonic. Urea crosses the membrane, so it accumulates inside, water follows it, and the cells lyse; 0.3 M urea is effectively hypotonic.
t: Osmolarity counts particles; tonicity counts only particles that can't get in.

q: Why is the equilibrium potential for Na⁺ positive (about +60 mV)?
o: Na⁺ is much more concentrated outside the cell
Na⁺ is more concentrated inside the cell
e: Na⁺ flows inward down its gradient until the inside becomes positive enough to stop it.
That balancing voltage is positive inside.

q: In cystic fibrosis, a defective CFTR protein causes thick, sticky mucus in the lungs. CFTR is a:
e: CFTR lets Cl⁻ exit epithelial cells, and water follows by osmosis.
Without it, secretions are dehydrated and thick.

q: The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pumps 30 Na⁺ ions out of a cell. How many ATP are used, and how many K⁺ come in?
e: Each cycle uses 1 ATP to move 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in.
30 Na⁺ ÷ 3 = 10 cycles → 10 ATP and 10 × 2 = 20 K⁺.

q: A patient with high blood potassium (hyperkalemia) is at risk for heart rhythm problems. How does raising extracellular [K⁺] affect a cardiac cell's resting membrane potential?
o: It becomes less negative (depolarizes), because the K⁺ gradient is smaller
It doesn't change, because the Na⁺/K⁺ pump compensates instantly
e: The resting potential is close to K⁺'s equilibrium potential, E = 61.5 log([K⁺]out/[K⁺]in).
Raising [K⁺]out makes that log less negative.
A partly depolarized cell has fewer recoverable Na⁺ channels, which disrupts normal heart rhythm.

q: Which junction seals neighboring epithelial cells so that solutes can't leak between them?
e: Tight junctions block the paracellular pathway (for example, in the blood–brain barrier and gut lining).
Gap junctions connect cytoplasms; desmosomes anchor cells to each other.

q: Which process releases substances from a cell by fusing vesicles with the plasma membrane?
e: Exocytosis: vesicles fuse with the membrane and release their contents outside (for example, neurotransmitters, hormones).

q: Compared with lateral diffusion within one leaflet, spontaneous 'flip-flop' of a phospholipid between leaflets is:
o: Very slow, because the polar head would have to cross the nonpolar core
Very fast, because the polar head is strongly attracted to the nonpolar core
About equally fast, because both depend only on temperature
Impossible, because phospholipids are anchored to membrane proteins
e: Phospholipids swap places with neighbors in their own leaflet millions of times per second.
Moving the charged head through the hydrocarbon core is so unfavorable that unaided flip-flop takes hours to days, which helps keep the two leaflets different.

q: A neuron rests at −70 mV, with Na⁺ much higher outside than inside. When Na⁺ channels open, which forces drive Na⁺ into the cell?
o: Both the concentration gradient and the negative interior
Only the concentration gradient; the voltage pushes Na⁺ out
Only the negative interior; the concentration gradient pushes Na⁺ out
Neither; Na⁺ enters only through the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase
e: Na⁺ diffuses from high (outside) to low (inside) concentration.
The negative inside also attracts the positive ion, so both parts of the electrochemical gradient point inward.

q: SGLT1 moves glucose into intestinal cells together with Na⁺, against glucose's concentration gradient. This is:
e: SGLT1 uses no ATP directly.
It uses the Na⁺ gradient made by the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase (which DOES use ATP). That makes it secondary active transport.

q: An anion-exchange column has positively charged beads. Which proteins bind to it?
o: Proteins with a net negative charge
Proteins with a net positive charge
e: Opposite charges attract: negative proteins stick to positive beads.
Bound proteins are released by raising the salt concentration or changing the pH.

q: Cyanogen bromide (CNBr) cuts a protein on the carboxyl side of each methionine. How many peptide fragments form from a single-chain protein with three internal Met residues (none at either end)?
e: Each cut adds one fragment to the original one chain.
3 cuts → 3 + 1 = 4 fragments.
t: n internal cuts in one linear chain → n + 1 pieces.

q: Collagen is best described as:
o: A fibrous structural protein with a triple-helix structure
A globular enzyme that breaks down connective tissue
A fibrous structural protein built from β-pleated sheets
A globular transport protein with four heme subunits
e: Collagen's three chains wind into a strong triple helix rich in Gly, Pro and hydroxyproline.
It gives strength to skin, tendons and bone.

q: Which method is best for finding the structure of a small protein while it moves freely in solution?
e: X-ray crystallography needs the protein packed in a crystal.
NMR works on proteins in solution, but mainly for smaller proteins.

q: Why does SDS-PAGE separate proteins by size rather than charge?
o: SDS gives every protein a similar negative charge per unit mass
SDS removes all native charges, leaving proteins uncharged
SDS coats proteins with a uniform positive charge per unit mass
At the gel's pH, every protein sits at its isoelectric point
e: SDS binds about evenly along the unfolded chain.
Its negative charge swamps the protein's own charge, so the charge-to-mass ratio is nearly the same for all proteins.
Only size then affects how fast they move through the gel.

q: Receptor A binds a ligand with K<sub>d</sub> = 1 nM; receptor B binds the same ligand with K<sub>d</sub> = 1 µM. Which statement is correct?
o: A binds the ligand about 1000 times more tightly
B binds the ligand about 1000 times more tightly
Both bind equally; K<sub>d</sub> only sets the speed
A binds faster but holds the ligand less tightly
e: K<sub>d</sub> is the ligand concentration giving 50% occupancy; lower K<sub>d</sub> = higher affinity.
1 µM / 1 nM = 1000, so A's affinity is about 1000 times greater.
t: Small K<sub>d</sub> = sticky. Think 'd' for 'dissociates': less dissociation, tighter binding.

q: A receptor binds a hormone with K<sub>d</sub> = 4 nM. What fraction of receptors is occupied when the free hormone concentration is 12 nM?
e: Fraction bound = [L]/(K<sub>d</sub> + [L]).

q: Which method determines a protein's three-dimensional atomic structure from the pattern a crystal makes when it scatters a beam?
e: Protein crystals diffract X-rays; the diffraction pattern is used to calculate an electron-density map and atomic positions.
NMR works in solution, not crystals.

q: Proteins marked for destruction by the proteasome are usually first tagged with chains of which small protein?
e: Enzymes attach chains of ubiquitin to lysine side chains of the target.
The 26S proteasome recognizes polyubiquitin, unfolds the protein, and cuts it into short peptides.

q: In size-exclusion (gel-filtration) chromatography, which proteins come off the column first?
e: Small proteins enter the beads' pores and take a longer path.
Large proteins are excluded from the pores and flow straight through, eluting first.

q: An antibody's antigen-binding site is formed by:
o: The variable regions of the heavy and light chains
The constant regions of the heavy chains
e: The tips of the antibody's Y have variable sequences that make each antibody specific.
The Fc (constant) region interacts with immune cells and complement.

q: A protein with pI = 6.0 is placed in a gel at pH 8.0 and an electric field is applied. Which way does it move?
o: Toward the anode (+), because it is negatively charged
Toward the cathode (−), because it is positively charged
Toward the cathode, because it is negatively charged
e: When pH > pI, the protein loses protons and carries a net negative charge.
Negative molecules move toward the positive electrode (anode).
t: pH above pI → negative. pH below pI → positive.

q: In the Haworth projection of α-D-glucopyranose, the –OH on the anomeric carbon is:
o: Trans to the CH₂OH group (pointing down)
Cis to the CH₂OH group (pointing up)
e: α: anomeric –OH on the opposite side from CH₂OH (down in a standard D-sugar Haworth).
β: same side as CH₂OH (up).
t: 'Alpha = axial = down' works for D-glucose drawn in the standard orientation.

q: Whether a sugar is D or L is determined by the configuration at:
o: The chiral carbon farthest from the carbonyl
The anomeric carbon formed when the ring closes
The chiral carbon closest to the carbonyl group
The majority of the chiral carbons in the chain
e: In a Fischer projection, if the –OH on the highest-numbered chiral carbon points right, the sugar is D.
For glucose, that carbon is C5.

q: Benedict's and Tollens' tests detect reducing sugars because these sugars:
o: Have an aldehyde (or can form one) that gets oxidized
Have a ketone group that gets reduced by the reagent
Have a glycosidic bond that the reagent hydrolyzes
Have an aldehyde group that gets reduced to an alcohol
e: The open-chain aldehyde is oxidized to a carboxylic acid.
The reagent is reduced: Cu²⁺ → Cu₂O (red precipitate) or Ag⁺ → Ag (silver mirror).

q: Complete hydrolysis of a linear amylose chain containing 500 glucose units requires how many water molecules?
e: A linear chain of 500 units has 500 − 1 = 499 glycosidic bonds.
Each hydrolysis uses one H₂O, so 499 waters are needed.

q: How does glycogen differ from amylopectin?
e: Both have α(1→4) chains with α(1→6) branches.
Glycogen branches about every 8–12 residues (amylopectin every 24–30), giving many ends for fast glucose release.

q: Fructose is classified as a:
e: Fructose has 6 carbons and a ketone at C2.

q: A patient feels bloating and gas after drinking milk. Which explanation fits best?
o: Low lactase lets undigested lactose reach colon bacteria, which ferment it
Excess lactase breaks lactose down too fast, flooding the gut with glucose
Milk proteins inhibit pancreatic amylase, so undigested starch reaches the colon
Low sucrase lets undigested sucrose reach the colon, where it is fermented
e: Without enough lactase, lactose can't be split into absorbable monosaccharides.
Colon bacteria ferment it, producing gas and drawing water into the gut (osmotic diarrhea).

q: In chair conformations, why is β-D-glucopyranose more stable than α-D-glucopyranose?
o: All its –OH and –CH₂OH groups can be equatorial
Its anomeric –OH is axial, away from the ring O
Its ring has fewer atoms, so there is less strain
Its anomeric carbon is not chiral, so it is symmetric
e: In β-D-glucose every large substituent, including the anomeric –OH, sits equatorial.
In α the anomeric –OH is axial, adding steric strain; this is why β is about 64% of the equilibrium mixture.

q: Starch is a polymer of which monosaccharide?
e: Starch (amylose and amylopectin), glycogen and cellulose are all glucose polymers. They differ in their linkages.

q: After glucose enters a cell, hexokinase converts it to glucose-6-phosphate. Why does this keep glucose inside the cell?
o: Its charged phosphate keeps it from crossing the membrane or using GLUT transporters
Phosphorylation makes it too large to pass through GLUT transporters
Phosphorylation links it into glycogen, which is too large to leave the cell
Phosphorylation converts it to fructose, which GLUT transporters cannot carry
e: GLUT transporters carry free glucose, not G6P.
The charged phosphate also prevents diffusion across the lipid bilayer.
This 'traps' glucose and keeps the internal free-glucose concentration low, so more can enter.

q: Reducing D-glucose with NaBH₄ gives one alditol, but reducing D-fructose gives two. Why?
o: Reducing fructose's C2 ketone creates a new chiral center
Fructose's ring opens two ways, giving two ketones
NaBH₄ also removes fructose's C1 –OH as water
Fructose first isomerizes to glucose and galactose
e: Glucose's C1 aldehyde becomes –CH₂OH, which is not chiral: one product (sorbitol).
Fructose's C2 becomes –CHOH– bonded to two different carbons, a new chiral center; hydride adds to either face, giving sorbitol and mannitol.

q: Which sugar is found in the backbone of DNA?
e: DNA's sugar lacks the –OH at C2′ (deoxy).
RNA uses ribose, which has a 2′-OH.

q: Steroid hormones like cortisol travel in the blood bound to carrier proteins. Why?
o: They are hydrophobic and dissolve poorly in plasma
They are too large to fit through capillaries
They would be hydrolyzed by blood enzymes
e: Steroids are lipids and don't dissolve well in water.
Carrier proteins transport them and create a reservoir; only the free fraction is active.

q: A patient receives fat-free intravenous nutrition for several weeks and develops scaly dermatitis and poor wound healing. Adding which lipid would most likely correct this?
e: Human desaturases cannot add double bonds beyond C9 (from the carboxyl end), so we cannot make linoleic (ω-6) or α-linolenic (ω-3) acid.
These essential fatty acids must come from the diet; the others listed can be made by the body.
t: Essential fatty acids: linoleic and α-linolenic. Oleic acid is NOT essential.

q: Which of these lipids is NOT built from isoprene units?
e: Cholesterol (via squalene), β-carotene (a tetraterpene) and retinol (from carotene) are all isoprenoids.
Palmitic acid is a fatty acid, built from two-carbon acetyl units by fatty acid synthase.

q: Phospholipase C cleaves the membrane lipid PIP₂. Which statement correctly describes the two products?
o: IP₃ diffuses to the ER to release Ca²⁺; DAG stays in the membrane to activate protein kinase C
DAG diffuses to the ER to release Ca²⁺; IP₃ stays in the membrane to activate protein kinase C
IP₃ and DAG both leave the cell and bind receptors on neighboring cells
IP₃ activates adenylyl cyclase, and DAG is stored in fat droplets
e: PIP₂ has a hydrophobic diacylglycerol part and a charged inositol trisphosphate head.
The soluble head (IP₃) moves through the cytosol to open ER Ca²⁺ channels; the hydrophobic DAG stays in the membrane, where it (with Ca²⁺) activates PKC.
t: Think solubility: the charged piece (IP₃) travels; the greasy piece (DAG) stays put.

q: Aspirin and ibuprofen reduce pain, fever and inflammation mainly by:
o: Inhibiting cyclooxygenase, which turns arachidonic acid into prostaglandins
Inhibiting lipoxygenase, which turns arachidonic acid into prostaglandins
Blocking the steroid hormone receptors that respond to prostaglandin signals
Activating phospholipase A₂ to remove arachidonic acid from the body
e: Cyclooxygenase (COX) catalyzes the first committed step from arachidonic acid to prostaglandins and thromboxanes.
NSAIDs block COX, so fewer prostaglandins are made. Lipoxygenase makes leukotrienes, not prostaglandins.

q: In Tay–Sachs disease, a lysosomal enzyme defect causes a sphingolipid that contains an oligosaccharide and sialic acid to build up in neurons. This lipid is a:
e: Gangliosides are glycosphingolipids with sialic acid in their sugar groups.
They are abundant in nerve cell membranes.

q: Vitamin A is needed for vision because it is converted to:
o: Retinal, the light-absorbing part of rhodopsin
Retinoic acid, which binds opsin to absorb light
A cofactor for carboxylating clotting proteins
e: Light changes 11-cis-retinal to all-trans-retinal, triggering the visual signal.
Deficiency causes night blindness.

q: Which vitamins are fat-soluble?
e: Fat-soluble vitamins are absorbed with dietary fats and stored in the liver and fat tissue, so they can build up to toxic levels.
B vitamins and vitamin C are water-soluble.

q: Which hormone is made from cholesterol?
e: Steroid hormones (cortisol, aldosterone, testosterone, estrogen) are made from cholesterol.
Insulin is a peptide; epinephrine and thyroxine come from tyrosine.

q: A sphingolipid whose polar head is a single sugar such as glucose or galactose is called a:
e: Ceramide + one monosaccharide = cerebroside.
Gangliosides carry an oligosaccharide with sialic acid; sphingomyelin carries phosphocholine; plasmalogens are glycerol-based ether lipids.
t: Cerebroside = one sugar; ganglioside = a sugar Gang (oligosaccharide + sialic acid).

q: Bile salts are released into the small intestine after a fatty meal. How do they help digestion?
o: They emulsify fat into small droplets, increasing the surface area for lipase
They hydrolyze triglycerides directly into free fatty acids and glycerol
They neutralize stomach acid so that pancreatic lipase can work in the gut
They are absorbed and oxidized as a major energy source after the meal
e: Bile salts are amphipathic, like detergents.
They break large fat globules into tiny droplets and micelles, so pancreatic lipase can reach more ester bonds.

q: Unlike phospholipids, triacylglycerols do not form bilayers in water. Why?
o: They have no charged or strongly polar head group
They are too water-soluble to stay together
Their three fatty acids are always fully saturated
They are too small to span half a bilayer
e: Bilayers need amphipathic molecules: a polar head facing water and nonpolar tails facing each other.
All three glycerol –OH groups of a TAG are esterified, leaving it almost entirely nonpolar, so it coalesces into oil droplets instead.

q: During fasting, glucagon mobilizes liver glycogen but not skeletal muscle glycogen. Why?
o: Skeletal muscle has essentially no glucagon receptors
Skeletal muscle cells lack glycogen phosphorylase
Glucagon can't leave the blood to reach muscle fibers
cAMP blocks glycogen breakdown inside muscle cells
e: Glucagon acts through a Gs-coupled receptor that is abundant in liver but essentially absent in skeletal muscle.
Muscle does have phosphorylase and responds to epinephrine (via β-adrenergic receptors and cAMP) and to Ca²⁺ and AMP.
Muscle glycogen is reserved for the muscle's own use.

q: Which tissue takes up glucose largely independently of insulin?
e: Neurons use GLUT1 and GLUT3, which are always in the membrane and have high affinity for glucose.
Muscle and fat rely on GLUT4, which moves to the membrane mainly in response to insulin (or, in muscle, exercise).
t: Brain, red cells and liver don't wait for insulin; muscle and fat (GLUT4) do.

q: AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) is turned on when the cell's AMP:ATP ratio rises. What does it do?
o: Activates ATP-making pathways and inhibits ATP-using ones like fatty acid synthesis
Activates ATP-using pathways like fatty acid synthesis and inhibits β-oxidation
Inhibits glucose uptake and glycolysis to conserve the cell's glucose stores
Shuts down all metabolic pathways until the AMP:ATP ratio returns to normal
e: AMPK is the cell's fuel gauge.
Low energy → AMPK switches on catabolism (glucose uptake, fat oxidation) and switches off anabolism.

q: A patient being overfed carbohydrate has a respiratory quotient (CO₂ produced ÷ O₂ consumed) above 1.0. What best explains this?
o: Converting carbohydrate to fat releases CO₂ without using O₂
Fat oxidation produces more CO₂ than O₂ it consumes
Protein oxidation gives an RQ well above 1.0
The lungs store extra O₂ when carbohydrate is abundant
e: Glucose oxidation alone gives RQ = 6 CO₂ ÷ 6 O₂ = 1.0.
Making fatty acids from carbohydrate releases CO₂ (e.g., pyruvate dehydrogenase) while the product, fat, is more reduced and holds less oxygen, so O₂ use doesn't keep pace.
Fat oxidation (≈0.7) and protein oxidation (≈0.8) give RQ below 1.

q: Why does ATP hydrolysis release so much free energy?
o: Its products are more stable, with less charge repulsion and more resonance
Breaking the phosphoanhydride bond itself releases a large amount of energy
Its products are less stable, with more charge repulsion and less resonance
ATP's phosphates are uncharged, so water attacks them very easily
e: ATP's neighboring negative phosphates repel each other.
Hydrolysis relieves this repulsion, and the products are better stabilized by resonance and hydration.

q: A person uses about 8,000 kJ of free energy as ATP each day. If each mole of ATP hydrolyzed in cells releases about 50 kJ and ATP's molar mass is about 500 g mol⁻¹, about how much ATP is recycled per day?
e: Moles of ATP = 8000 kJ ÷ 50 kJ mol⁻¹ = 160 mol.
Mass = 160 mol × 0.5 kg mol⁻¹ = 80 kg.
The body holds only a small ATP pool at any moment, so each ATP is regenerated hundreds of times a day.

q: Which sign of ΔG indicates a thermodynamically favorable process under specified conditions?
e: A negative Gibbs free-energy change indicates thermodynamic favorability.

q: Cells build highly ordered macromolecules from simpler molecules. Why doesn't this violate the second law of thermodynamics?
o: Cells release heat and small molecules, raising total entropy
Living cells are isolated systems that are exempt from the law
Enzymes directly lower the total entropy of the universe
Building macromolecules raises entropy inside the cell itself
e: Cells are open systems that exchange matter and energy with their surroundings.
Breaking down fuels to CO₂ and H₂O and giving off heat increases the surroundings' entropy more than biosynthesis decreases the cell's.
So the entropy of cell + surroundings still increases.

q: Metabolic pathways are usually regulated at enzymes whose reactions are far from equilibrium. Why?
o: Their large negative ΔG means changing their activity changes pathway flux
Near-equilibrium enzymes are too slow to affect pathway flux at all
Far-from-equilibrium steps are easily reversed by mass action
Enzymes near equilibrium can't bind allosteric effectors
e: A near-equilibrium step runs both ways quickly; its net direction simply follows substrate and product levels.
A far-from-equilibrium step (ΔG ≪ 0) is effectively one-way and often slow, so it limits flux; speeding it up or slowing it down controls the whole pathway.
Examples: hexokinase, PFK-1, pyruvate kinase, isocitrate dehydrogenase.

q: After a carbohydrate-rich meal, which process does insulin promote?
o: Glycogen synthesis in liver and muscle
e: Insulin turns on storage: glycogen synthesis, fatty acid synthesis and GLUT4-mediated glucose uptake.

q: Leptin, a hormone released by fat tissue, acts on the hypothalamus to:
o: Decrease appetite and signal that energy stores are adequate
Increase appetite and signal that energy stores are running low
Raise blood glucose directly by stimulating liver gluconeogenesis
Promote fat storage by stimulating insulin release from the pancreas
e: More fat → more leptin → reduced appetite.
Ghrelin, from the stomach, does the opposite: it increases hunger.

q: Insulin activates protein phosphatase 1 (PP1) in liver and muscle. How does this shift glycogen metabolism?
o: Dephosphorylation activates glycogen synthase and inactivates phosphorylase
Dephosphorylation activates phosphorylase and inactivates glycogen synthase
Phosphorylation activates both glycogen synthase and phosphorylase
Dephosphorylation inactivates both enzymes until glucagon returns
e: Glycogen synthase is active when dephosphorylated; glycogen phosphorylase is active when phosphorylated.
By removing phosphates, PP1 turns synthesis on and breakdown off: insulin's 'store glucose' signal.
t: Phosphorylation (glucagon, epinephrine) = break down glycogen. Dephosphorylation (insulin) = build it.

q: In pyruvate kinase deficiency, intermediates upstream of the block build up in red blood cells, including 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate (shown). How does this affect hemoglobin?
o: O₂ affinity falls, so more O₂ is unloaded to tissues
O₂ affinity rises, shifting the curve to the left
O₂ affinity is unchanged, since 2,3-BPG binds only HbF
Hemoglobin binds CO₂ at the heme in place of O₂
e: RBCs make 2,3-BPG from the glycolytic intermediate 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate (bisphosphoglycerate mutase).
2,3-BPG binds deoxyhemoglobin and stabilizes the T state, shifting the O₂ curve to the right.
This partly offsets the anemia; HbF actually binds 2,3-BPG poorly.

q: In the Fischer projection shown, is this sugar D or L, and why?
o: D, because the –OH on C5 points right
L, because the –OH on C3 points left
D, because the –OH on C2 points right
L, because the CHO is at the top
e: D/L is set by the chiral carbon farthest from the carbonyl (C5).
Its –OH points to the right → D (this is D-glucose).

e: Same x-intercept (−1/Km) → Km unchanged.
Higher y-intercept (1/Vmax) → Vmax lowered.

q: The disaccharide shown (two glucose units) gives a negative Benedict's test. What explains this?
o: Both anomeric carbons are tied up in the glycosidic bond
It has no free –OH groups on either ring to oxidize
Its glucose units are L sugars, which do not react
Its β(1→4) bond is too stable for Benedict's reagent
e: A reducing sugar needs a free hemiacetal that can open to an aldehyde.
Here C1 of one glucose is bonded through O to C1 of the other (an α,α-1,1 link, as in trehalose), so neither ring can open.

q: Which citric acid cycle enzyme converts citrate (shown) into its isomer, isocitrate?
e: Aconitase removes and re-adds water (via cis-aconitate), moving the OH group from a tertiary carbon to a secondary carbon.
A secondary alcohol can be oxidized by isocitrate dehydrogenase; citrate's tertiary alcohol cannot.

q: A protein runs at about 75 kDa on SDS-PAGE without a reducing agent, but as bands of about 50 and 25 kDa with β-mercaptoethanol (βME). What does this suggest?
o: Its 50 and 25 kDa subunits are joined by disulfides
It is a single 66 kDa chain that breaks apart in SDS
βME added 9 kDa of mass to the protein
The protein is not affected by reducing agents
e: βME breaks disulfide bonds, separating subunits.
50 + 25 = 75 kDa, the size of the intact protein.

e: It has a base (adenine) attached to a sugar, but no phosphate group, so it is a nucleoside, not a nucleotide.

t: Nucleoside = base + sugar. Nucleotide = nucleoside + phosphate.
