q: The movement of alleles from one population to another through migration and interbreeding is called:
e: Gene flow transfers alleles between populations.
It tends to make populations more genetically similar to each other.

q: In a population at Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium, 1 in 10,000 people has a recessive disease. About what fraction are carriers?
A woman whose father had hemophilia (X-linked recessive) has children with an unaffected man. What is the chance that their son has hemophilia?
e: She must be a carrier (she got her father's X).
A son gets one of her two X's, so there's a 1/2 chance he gets the affected one.

q: In a population of seed-eating birds, both small-beaked and large-beaked birds survive well, but birds with medium beaks do poorly. Which type of selection is acting?
e: Disruptive selection favors both extremes over the middle.
Over time it can split the population into two distinct forms.

q: The observable traits of an organism are its:
e: Genotype: the alleles. Phenotype: the expressed traits.

q: A woman who is a carrier of an X-linked recessive disorder has children with an unaffected man. What is the probability that a son will be affected?
e: Mother: XᴬXᵃ. Father: XᴬY.
A son always gets Y from dad and one X from mom.
Mom passes Xᵃ half the time, so P(affected son) = ½.
t: Read carefully: 'probability a son is affected' (½) differs from 'probability a child is an affected son' (¼).

q: A hurricane kills most of an island's lizards at random, and the few survivors carry only a small fraction of the original alleles. This is an example of:
e: A bottleneck is a sharp drop in population size that randomly removes alleles.
The founder effect is similar, but happens when a small group leaves to start a new population.

q: A sample of 100 plants contains 50 AA, 20 Aa and 30 aa individuals. How does the number of heterozygotes compare with the Hardy–Weinberg expectation?
o: Far fewer than expected, as with inbreeding
Far more than expected, as with heterozygote advantage
About the same as expected, so the population is in equilibrium
It can't be compared without knowing the mutation rate
e: Expected heterozygotes = 2pq = 2 × 0.6 × 0.4 = 0.48 (48 plants), but only 20 are observed.
A heterozygote shortage suggests inbreeding (for example, self-pollination) or population subdivision.

q: The founder effect happens when:
o: A small group starts a new population with different allele frequencies
A disaster suddenly shrinks a large population to a few survivors
Many migrants move in and add new alleles to an existing population
Selection favors heterozygotes, keeping both alleles common
e: It's a type of genetic drift, often seen in isolated communities.

q: Human birth weight shows that very small and very large babies have lower survival, while medium weights do best. This is:
e: Selection favors the middle and acts against both extremes.

q: For two unlinked genes, a cross is made between AaBb and aabb. What fraction of the offspring are aabb?
e: Each gene separately: Aa × aa gives ½ aa, and Bb × bb gives ½ bb.
Unlinked genes assort independently: ½ × ½ = ¼

q: Structures that look different but share a common evolutionary origin, like a human arm and a bat wing, are:
e: Analogous structures (like bird and insect wings) have similar function but different origins.

q: How does bacterial binary fission differ from eukaryotic mitosis?
o: It occurs with no spindle and no nuclear envelope
It produces two genetically different cells
It requires homologous chromosomes to pair up
It occurs only after a round of conjugation
e: Bacteria have no nucleus and no mitotic spindle. The single circular chromosome is copied and the two copies are moved apart as the cell grows and pinches in two.
Like mitosis, it produces two genetically identical cells (barring mutations).

q: Which cytoskeletal element forms the mitotic spindle?
e: Microtubules (tubulin polymers) form the spindle, cilia, flagella and tracks for motor proteins.

q: Which organelle detoxifies drugs and makes lipids such as steroids?
e: Smooth ER lacks ribosomes.
It makes lipids and steroids and, in liver cells, detoxifies drugs.

q: A Staphylococcus strain resists penicillin. Adding clavulanic acid, which inhibits β-lactamase, does not restore penicillin's effect. Which resistance mechanism fits best?
o: Altered penicillin-binding proteins with low drug affinity
A β-lactamase enzyme that hydrolyzes penicillin
Complete loss of the peptidoglycan cell wall
An outer membrane that blocks drug entry
e: If β-lactamase caused the resistance, blocking it with clavulanic acid would restore killing; it did not.
Staphylococcus is Gram-positive, so it has no outer membrane, and it still needs its peptidoglycan wall.
The remaining explanation is a changed target: penicillin-binding proteins (wall-building enzymes) that the drug no longer binds well, as in MRSA.

q: Mitochondria have their own circular DNA and 70S-like ribosomes. These features support which idea?
o: Cell theory's claim that all cells have nuclei
e: Mitochondria resemble bacteria that were engulfed by an ancestral cell.
Chloroplasts share the same features.

q: A bacterial culture in steady log-phase growth rises from 1.0 × 10³ to 8.0 × 10³ cells in 90 minutes. What is its doubling time?
e: 8.0 × 10³ ÷ 1.0 × 10³ = 8 = 2³, so the population doubled 3 times.
Doubling time = 90 min ÷ 3 = 30 minutes.
t: 11 minutes comes from dividing by 8; count doublings, not the fold-increase.

q: A mutation deletes the nuclear localization signal from a large transcription factor made on free cytosolic ribosomes. Where will most of the protein end up?
e: Large proteins enter the nucleus through nuclear pores only if they carry a nuclear localization signal.
The protein has no ER signal sequence either (it is made on free ribosomes), so it stays in the cytosol, where it cannot reach its target genes.

q: A patient's illness is caused by a prion. What makes prions unusual infectious agents?
o: They are misfolded proteins that convert normal proteins, with no DNA or RNA
They are tiny viruses whose RNA genome has no protective protein coat
They are wall-less bacteria that hide and replicate inside host neurons
They are DNA fragments that insert into and disrupt neuron genomes
e: Prions spread by templating their abnormal shape onto normal copies of the same protein.
Because they are very stable protein aggregates with no DNA or RNA, prions resist standard sterilization (such as routine autoclaving) and need harsher treatment.

q: A bacterial population doubles every 20 minutes. Starting with 100 cells under ideal conditions, how many are there after 2 hours?
e: 2 hours = 120 min = 6 doublings.

q: In a tube of thioglycolate broth, O₂ is highest at the top and falls to almost zero at the bottom. A bacterium grows only in a band at the very bottom. It is most likely:
e: Obligate aerobes grow only at the top; facultative anaerobes grow throughout but best near the top.
Aerotolerant anaerobes ignore O₂ and grow evenly.
Growth only where O₂ is absent means O₂ is toxic to the cell: an obligate anaerobe.

q: Which eukaryotic organelle is most directly responsible for oxidative ATP synthesis?
e: The inner mitochondrial membrane houses oxidative phosphorylation complexes.

q: Which organelle contains enzymes that break down worn-out organelles and engulfed material?
e: Lysosomes hold acid hydrolases that work best at pH about 5.
They digest material from endocytosis and autophagy.

q: Down syndrome risk rises with maternal age. Based on oogenesis, which explanation is most reasonable?
o: Oocytes arrest in meiosis for decades, so nondisjunction is likelier when it resumes
Older women make new oocytes by mitosis, and these are more error-prone
Older mothers' embryos divide more slowly by mitosis, causing chromosome loss
Aging oocytes accumulate point mutations in genes on chromosome 21
e: All primary oocytes form before birth and pause in prophase I.
The longer the pause, the more likely chromosome separation errors become.

q: A bodybuilder takes high doses of synthetic androgens for a year. Tests show low LH and FSH, a low sperm count and smaller testes. What best explains these findings?
o: Negative feedback from the androgens suppressed GnRH, LH and FSH
The androgens directly destroyed the anterior pituitary
Excess testosterone overstimulated and exhausted the Leydig cells
The androgens blocked androgen receptors in the testes
e: High circulating androgens feed back on the hypothalamus and pituitary, lowering GnRH, LH and FSH.
Low LH means Leydig cells make little testosterone inside the testes, and low FSH reduces Sertoli support, so sperm production falls and the testes shrink.

q: Sertoli cells secrete inhibin. If a drug blocked inhibin's action, which hormone change would most directly follow?
e: Inhibin provides negative feedback mainly on FSH release from the anterior pituitary.
Removing that feedback lets FSH rise.

q: If no embryo implants, what most directly triggers menstruation at the end of the ovarian cycle?
o: Progesterone falls as the corpus luteum breaks down
Estrogen rises sharply as new follicles mature
An LH surge causes the lining to detach
hCG rises and breaks down the endometrium
e: Without hCG from an embryo, the corpus luteum degenerates about 2 weeks after ovulation.
Progesterone (and estrogen) levels drop, the endometrium loses its hormonal support, and the lining is shed.

q: The Rb protein binds the transcription factor E2F; phosphorylation of Rb by cyclin D–CDK4/6 releases E2F to turn on S-phase genes. What is the most likely effect of losing both copies of the Rb gene?
o: Cells pass the G₁/S checkpoint without proper signals
Cells arrest permanently in G₁ and stop dividing
Cells skip S phase and divide without copying DNA
Cells can no longer separate their duplicated sister chromatids
e: Unphosphorylated Rb acts as a brake by holding E2F.
With no Rb, E2F is always free, so S-phase genes switch on even without growth signals: Rb is a tumor suppressor.

q: In an unsynchronized culture with a 20-hour cell cycle, 5% of the cells are in mitosis at any moment. About how long does mitosis last?
e: In an unsynchronized culture, the fraction of cells in a phase equals the fraction of the cycle spent in that phase.
Time in mitosis = 0.05 × 20 h = 1 hour.

q: In pregnancy, what keeps the corpus luteum from breaking down in the first trimester?
e: hCG acts like LH to keep the corpus luteum making progesterone.
Pregnancy tests detect hCG.

q: Nondisjunction during meiosis can cause:
o: Gametes with an extra or missing chromosome
Gametes with swapped segments between homologs
Gametes with a single base-pair point mutation
Embryos that split to form identical twins
e: Failure of chromosomes to separate gives n + 1 and n − 1 gametes.
Fertilization by an n + 1 gamete can cause trisomy, like trisomy 21 (Down syndrome).

q: After ovulation, the corpus luteum mainly secretes:
e: Progesterone keeps the uterine lining ready for implantation.
If no pregnancy occurs, the corpus luteum breaks down and menstruation follows.

q: The acrosome at the tip of a sperm head contains:
o: Enzymes that help it get through the egg's outer layers
Mitochondria that power the steady beating of the flagellum
Glycogen that fuels the sperm as it swims to the egg
Ribosomes that make proteins for the early embryo
e: The acrosome is a cap-like vesicle derived from the Golgi.
On contact with the egg, it releases enzymes that digest a path through the zona pellucida (the acrosome reaction).
Mitochondria sit in the midpiece, not the head.

q: At birth, a human female's primary oocytes are arrested in:
e: Primary oocytes pause in prophase I from before birth; starting at puberty, one resumes meiosis I each cycle just before ovulation, so some stay arrested for decades.
At ovulation, the secondary oocyte is arrested in metaphase II and finishes meiosis only if fertilized.

q: Independent assortment occurs when:
o: Homologous pairs line up randomly at metaphase I
Sister chromatids separate in anaphase II
DNA is copied in S phase
e: Each homolog pair's orientation is random, giving 2²³ (over 8 million) possible chromosome combinations in human gametes.

q: A drug taken in the first trimester causes limb malformations, but the same dose in the third trimester does not. What best explains this?
o: Limbs and organs form in the first trimester, the period most sensitive to teratogens
The placenta forms only in the third trimester, so early drugs reach the fetus freely
The fetus has no circulation in the first trimester, so drugs accumulate in tissues
Drugs can't cross the placenta in the third trimester, so the fetus is unexposed
e: Organogenesis happens mostly in weeks 3–8.
This is when teratogens (like thalidomide) cause major structural defects.

q: A zygote completes four rounds of cleavage with no growth. Compared with the zygote, about what volume does each cell have?
e: Four doublings give 2⁴ = 16 cells.
With no growth, the zygote's volume is shared 16 ways, so each cell has about 1/16 of it.

q: A person's neurons and liver cells make very different proteins, yet carry the same genome. What best explains this?
o: Each cell type expresses a different set of genes
Each cell type deletes the genes it does not use
Neurons and liver cells carry different mutations
Neurons read codons with a different genetic code
e: Differentiation comes from differential gene expression, not from changes to the DNA itself.
Transcription factors and chromatin states switch on liver genes in liver cells and neuronal genes in neurons.

q: Scientists turn adult skin cells into induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs). Why are these useful in medicine?
o: They can become many cell types and match the patient's own genome
They are totipotent, so they can also form placental tissue
They never form tumors, since they come from adult cells
They can become only skin cells, which simplifies grafting
e: iPSCs are reprogrammed with a few transcription factors.
Because they come from the patient, transplants may avoid immune rejection.

q: In deuterostomes such as humans, the blastopore that forms during gastrulation becomes the:
e: Deuterostome means 'second mouth': the blastopore becomes the anus and the mouth forms later at the other end.
In protostomes (such as most invertebrates), the blastopore becomes the mouth.

q: An infant has severe constipation because one segment of the colon lacks the nerve cells normally found in its wall. Failed migration of which embryonic cells best explains this?
e: The enteric nervous system (the gut's own neurons) is built from neural crest cells that migrate along the gut.
If they fail to reach the end of the colon, that segment cannot push stool along (Hirschsprung disease).

q: Which germ layer gives rise to the nervous system?
e: Ectoderm forms the epidermis and the nervous system (via the neural tube).
Mesoderm forms muscle, bone, blood and kidneys.
Endoderm forms the gut lining, liver, pancreas and lungs.
t: Ectoderm = 'attract-o-derm': skin and nerves, the parts that interact with the world.

q: Which vessel carries oxygen-rich blood from the placenta to the fetus?
e: Umbilical vein: oxygenated blood toward the fetus.
Umbilical arteries: deoxygenated blood back to the placenta.
t: Fetal circulation flips the usual rule that arteries carry oxygen-rich blood.

q: Sickle cell disease is caused by a mutation in the β-globin gene. Affected infants usually have few symptoms until about 6 months of age. What best explains this delay?
o: Fetal hemoglobin (α₂γ₂), which lacks β chains, still dominates
Antibodies from the mother destroy sickled red cells until then
The β-globin gene acquires its mutation only after birth
Newborn red cells contain no hemoglobin for six months
e: Before birth, red cells mostly contain HbF, made of two α and two γ chains, so the mutant β chain is barely used.
After birth, γ-globin production switches to β-globin over several months; as HbS replaces HbF, sickling begins.
t: This is why the drug hydroxyurea, which raises HbF, eases sickle cell disease.

q: Fertilization usually occurs in the:
e: The egg is fertilized in the ampulla of the fallopian tube, then travels to the uterus.

q: A patient receives a transplant of hematopoietic stem cells. Which cells can these donor stem cells normally replace?
o: Red cells, white cells and platelets
Blood cells as well as neurons and liver cells
Red blood cells only, but not white cells
Lymphocytes only, but not red blood cells
e: Hematopoietic stem cells are multipotent: they produce every blood cell lineage (myeloid and lymphoid).
They are not pluripotent, so they do not normally make tissues such as neurons or hepatocytes.

q: What is the fluid-filled cavity inside a blastula (or blastocyst) called?
e: The blastocoel forms as cells of the morula pump fluid inward.
The archenteron is the primitive gut that forms later, during gastrulation.

q: Which cells make myelin in the central nervous system?
e: CNS: oligodendrocytes. PNS: Schwann cells.

q: Which brain structure is most important for forming new long-term explicit memories?
e: Damage to the hippocampus causes anterograde amnesia: trouble forming new memories.

q: What neurotransmitter is released at the neuromuscular junction of skeletal muscle?
e: ACh binds nicotinic receptors on the muscle, triggering depolarization.

q: The sympathetic nervous system is responsible for:
e: Sympathetic: faster heart rate, dilated pupils, less digestion.
Parasympathetic: rest and digest.

q: Which receptor type converts light into nerve signals?
e: Photoreceptors contain light-sensitive pigments (opsins with retinal).

q: The rapid depolarization (rising phase) of an action potential is caused by:
e: At threshold, voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open.
Na⁺ rushes in down its electrochemical gradient.
The inside quickly becomes positive. Repolarization then comes from K⁺ flowing out.
t: Na⁺ in = up. K⁺ out = down.

q: A neuron rests at −70 mV with a threshold of −55 mV. At the same moment, its axon hillock receives three EPSPs of +6 mV each and one IPSP of −4 mV. Assuming the potentials simply add, what happens?
o: It reaches −56 mV and does not fire
It reaches −60 mV and does not fire
e: Net change = 3(+6) + (−4) = +14 mV.
−70 + 14 = −56 mV, which is still 1 mV short of the −55 mV threshold, so no action potential.
t: −52 mV forgets the IPSP; −48 mV adds it in the wrong direction.

q: Ependymal cells line the brain's ventricles. What do they help produce?
e: Ependymal cells, especially in the choroid plexus, help make and circulate cerebrospinal fluid (CSF).
CSF cushions the brain and spinal cord.

q: Which brainstem region controls breathing and heart rate?
e: The medulla contains centers for breathing, heart rate and blood pressure.

q: In the knee-jerk reflex, tapping the tendon stretches the quadriceps. Which statement is correct?
o: A sensory neuron synapses directly on a motor neuron in the spinal cord
The signal must reach the brain before the quadriceps can contract
An interneuron must relay the signal to the quadriceps motor neuron
The cerebellum detects the stretch and directly triggers contraction
e: The patellar reflex is monosynaptic.
The brain is informed afterward, but it isn't needed for the reflex.

q: Multiple sclerosis damages myelin in the CNS. Which symptom pattern fits best?
o: Slowed or blocked nerve conduction, causing weakness and vision problems
Muscle cells unable to contract even when stimulated
e: Without myelin, action potentials slow or fail.
Symptoms depend on where the damage is, often including vision and movement.

q: How does myelination by Schwann cells differ from myelination by oligodendrocytes?
o: Each Schwann cell wraps one axon segment; each oligodendrocyte wraps segments of many axons
Schwann cells myelinate CNS axons; oligodendrocytes myelinate PNS axons
Only myelin made by oligodendrocytes has nodes of Ranvier
Schwann cell myelin contains no lipid, unlike oligodendrocyte myelin
e: Schwann cells myelinate axons in the PNS, and each one wraps a single segment of a single axon.
Oligodendrocytes work in the CNS and extend several processes, each myelinating a segment of a different axon. Both kinds of myelin are lipid-rich and leave nodes of Ranvier.

q: A hormone has a plasma half-life of 10 minutes. If its secretion stops when its level is 80 pg/mL, what is the level 30 minutes later?
e: 30 minutes is 3 half-lives (30 ÷ 10 = 3).
t: Halve once per half-life; don't divide by the number of half-lives (80 ÷ 3 ≈ 27 is the trap).

q: Which is an example of positive feedback?
e: Contractions trigger more oxytocin, which strengthens contractions, until birth ends the loop.

q: A patient with Graves' disease has antibodies that activate the TSH receptor. Which lab pattern is expected?
e: The antibodies stimulate the thyroid directly, raising T₄.
High T₄ then suppresses pituitary TSH by negative feedback.

q: Iodine deficiency can cause a goiter (enlarged thyroid). Why?
o: Too little thyroid hormone raises TSH, which overstimulates the thyroid
Iodine shortage makes thyroid cells inflame and swell from damage
TSH falls to zero, so the gland swells with unused colloid
The thyroid hoards extra iodine, which expands the follicles
e: Thyroid hormone needs iodine.
Low hormone → high TSH → thyroid growth.

q: A pituitary tumor begins secreting excess growth hormone in a 40-year-old man. His hands, feet and jaw slowly enlarge, but he does not grow taller. Why?
o: His growth plates have fused, so long bones can't lengthen
Growth hormone acts only on the bones of the hands and face
Excess growth hormone blocks IGF-1 production by the liver
Adults lack growth hormone receptors on their bone cells
e: Growth hormone, acting largely through IGF-1 from the liver, stimulates bone and soft-tissue growth.
After puberty the epiphyseal plates have fused, so bones can only thicken and soft tissues enlarge (acromegaly); before fusion the same tumor causes gigantism.
t: GH excess before the plates close → gigantism; after → acromegaly.

q: Calcitonin and PTH work as antagonists. If blood calcium is too high, which response is expected?
e: Calcitonin lowers blood calcium (bone deposition).
PTH raises it, so it would be reduced.

q: Rising cortisol inhibits CRH and ACTH release. This is an example of:
e: The output (cortisol) shuts down its own production pathway, keeping levels stable.

q: The parafollicular (C) cells of the thyroid secrete which hormone?
e: Thyroid follicular cells make T₄ and T₃; the parafollicular C cells between follicles make calcitonin.
PTH comes from the separate parathyroid glands, and TSH comes from the anterior pituitary.
t: C cells make Calcitonin, which lowers blood Calcium.

q: An autoimmune attack destroys a patient's adrenal cortex (Addison disease). Which set of findings is expected?
o: High ACTH, low blood Na⁺ and high blood K⁺
Low ACTH, high blood Na⁺ and low blood K⁺
High ACTH, high blood Na⁺ and low blood K⁺
Low ACTH, low blood Na⁺ and high blood K⁺
e: Low cortisol removes negative feedback, so the pituitary makes much more ACTH.
Without aldosterone, the kidney loses Na⁺ in the urine and keeps K⁺, so blood Na⁺ falls and K⁺ rises.
t: Addison = adrenal cortex gone: low cortisol and aldosterone, high ACTH, and skin darkening from ACTH's precursor.

q: Which hormone does the adrenal medulla secrete?
e: Medulla: epinephrine and norepinephrine (fight or flight).
Cortex: cortisol, aldosterone and androgens.

q: A runner drinks a lot of plain water during a marathon and develops low blood Na⁺. Which hormone response would the body show to correct the dilute blood?
e: Dilute blood lowers plasma osmolarity.
The hypothalamus reduces ADH, so the kidneys excrete more dilute urine.

q: A tumor in the adrenal cortex secretes too much aldosterone. Which findings are expected?
o: High blood pressure and low blood K⁺
Low blood pressure and high blood K⁺
e: Aldosterone holds Na⁺ (and water), raising blood pressure.
It also increases K⁺ excretion, lowering blood K⁺.

q: What is the main chemical stimulus that drives breathing rate in a healthy person?
o: Rising CO₂ (and H⁺) in the blood
Falling O₂ (and H⁺) in the blood
Rising O₂ (and HCO₃⁻) in the blood
Falling CO₂ (and H⁺) in the blood
e: Central chemoreceptors in the medulla respond to pH changes caused by CO₂.
Low O₂ becomes the main driver only when it's very low.

q: What does pulmonary surfactant do?
o: Lowers surface tension in the alveoli
Traps inhaled particles in the bronchi
Carries O₂ across the alveolar wall
e: It keeps small alveoli from collapsing.

q: In pneumonia, some alveoli fill with fluid but still receive blood flow. Why does breathing 100% O₂ raise arterial P(O₂) only a little?
o: Blood through those alveoli never meets the added O₂
Fluid in the alveoli absorbs most of the extra O₂
Hemoglobin cannot bind O₂ in pneumonia patients
Extra O₂ slows breathing, so ventilation drops
e: Fluid-filled alveoli are perfused but not ventilated (a shunt), so their blood stays deoxygenated.
Blood from healthy alveoli is already nearly 100% saturated and can't carry much more, so mixing still gives low arterial P(O₂).

q: A patient with emphysema has damaged alveolar walls. Which change best explains their trouble with gas exchange?
o: Less alveolar surface area for diffusion
e: Emphysema destroys alveolar walls, merging them into larger, fewer air spaces.

q: Blood has 15 g of hemoglobin per dL. Each gram binds up to 1.34 mL of O₂, and saturation is 100%. About how much O₂ is bound to hemoglobin per dL of blood?
e: O₂ bound = 15 g/dL × 1.34 mL/g × 1.00.
15 × 1.34 ≈ 20 mL O₂ per dL of blood.

q: Premature babies often have respiratory distress. What is the most likely cause?
o: Too little surfactant, so the alveoli collapse
Too much surfactant, so the alveoli overexpand
Too much fetal hemoglobin, so O₂ can't be released to tissues
An open ductus venosus, so blood bypasses the lungs
e: Surfactant production rises late in pregnancy (around weeks 28–36).
Steroids given to the mother can speed lung maturation.

q: Which change shifts the oxygen–hemoglobin dissociation curve to the right?
e: A right shift means hemoglobin releases O₂ more easily (lower affinity).
This happens with more CO₂, more H⁺ (lower pH), higher temperature and more 2,3-BPG.
That's exactly the situation in exercising muscle, where O₂ is needed.
t: Bohr effect: active tissue is hot, acidic and full of CO₂, so hemoglobin unloads O₂ there.

q: Why does gas exchange occur so efficiently across the alveolar wall?
o: Its thin wall and huge surface area allow rapid diffusion
Active transport pumps move O₂ into the capillary blood
Its thick wall stores O₂ for steady release into blood
Air pressure forces O₂ into the blood by bulk flow
e: Fick's law: diffusion rises with surface area and falls with wall thickness.

q: Most CO₂ is carried in the blood as:
o: CO₂ bound to iron in hemoglobin
e: Carbonic anhydrase in red blood cells converts CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃ → H⁺ + HCO₃⁻.
About 70% of CO₂ travels this way.

q: In systemic capillaries, HCO₃⁻ formed inside red blood cells moves out into the plasma. Which ion moves in to balance the charge?
e: A band 3 exchanger swaps HCO₃⁻ out for Cl⁻ in (the chloride shift), so the cell stays electrically neutral.
The H⁺ made alongside HCO₃⁻ stays inside, buffered by hemoglobin.

q: At rest, normal exhalation is mainly caused by:
o: Passive elastic recoil of the stretched lungs
Active contraction of the diaphragm upward
Contraction of the external intercostal muscles
Strong contraction of the abdominal muscles
e: During quiet breathing, the diaphragm simply relaxes and the stretched lungs recoil, pushing air out.
Abdominal and internal intercostal muscles are used only for forced exhalation; external intercostals help inhalation.
t: The diaphragm never pushes up actively: it contracts (down) to inhale and relaxes to exhale.

q: Where does gas exchange occur in the lungs?
e: Alveoli have thin walls and a huge surface area, surrounded by capillaries.

q: A patient with kidney failure develops anemia. Which explanation fits best?
o: The damaged kidneys make too little erythropoietin
The kidneys filter out red blood cells
Bone marrow makes too many red blood cells
e: EPO drives red blood cell production; patients often receive EPO injections.

q: Which blood test is often used to estimate how well the kidneys filter?
e: Creatinine is freely filtered and barely reabsorbed, so its level reflects the glomerular filtration rate.

q: ACE inhibitors are blood pressure medicines. How do they work?
o: They block conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II
They block renin release from the juxtaglomerular cells
They block aldosterone receptors in the collecting duct
They block conversion of angiotensinogen to angiotensin I
e: Less angiotensin II → less vasoconstriction and less aldosterone → lower blood pressure.

q: Where is most of the filtered glucose reabsorbed?
e: The proximal tubule reabsorbs nearly all glucose and amino acids and most Na⁺ and water.

q: Which region of the kidney contains the glomeruli and the convoluted tubules?
e: Glomeruli, Bowman's capsules and the proximal and distal convoluted tubules all sit in the outer cortex.
The medulla holds the loops of Henle and collecting ducts; the pelvis collects urine.

q: Why does drinking alcohol increase urination?
e: Less ADH → fewer aquaporins in the collecting duct → more dilute urine.

q: The loop of Henle's main role is to:
o: Create a salt gradient in the medulla so concentrated urine can form
Filter blood plasma into the tubule under hydrostatic pressure
Secrete renin and erythropoietin to regulate blood pressure
Reabsorb all filtered glucose and amino acids into the blood
e: The countercurrent multiplier pumps salt out of the ascending limb, making the medulla salty.
Water then leaves the collecting duct when ADH is present.

q: During a fever, the hypothalamus raises the body's temperature set point. While body temperature is still climbing toward the new set point, what does the patient experience?
o: Feeling cold, with shivering and pale skin
Feeling hot, with sweating and flushed skin
Feeling hot, with shivering and flushed skin
No sensation until the new set point is reached
e: The body is now below its new set point, so it acts as if it's cold.
It shivers to make heat and constricts skin vessels to save heat (chills); sweating comes later when the fever 'breaks'.

q: If blood glucose is very high, glucose appears in the urine. Why?
o: The loop of Henle secretes glucose
e: Reabsorption has a maximum (transport maximum).
Above about 180–200 mg dL⁻¹, extra glucose spills into urine.

q: Glomerular filtration rate (GFR) is 125 mL min⁻¹. About how much filtrate is made per day?
e: About 99% is reabsorbed, leaving 1–2 L of urine.

q: What is the main role of the vasa recta, the capillaries that run alongside the loops of Henle?
o: Supplying the medulla without washing out its salt gradient
Filtering blood plasma into Bowman's capsule
Secreting renin when blood pressure drops
Carrying urine from the collecting ducts to the pelvis
e: The vasa recta run down and back up in a hairpin, like the loop of Henle (countercurrent exchange).
Solutes entering on the way down leave on the way up, so the medulla stays salty while still getting O₂ and nutrients.

q: At the cellular level, how does ADH increase water reabsorption in the collecting duct?
o: It causes aquaporin channels to be inserted into the membrane
It powers an ATP pump that moves water directly
It makes the duct secrete more Na⁺ into the urine
It widens the pores of the glomerular filter
e: ADH binds V₂ receptors, raising cAMP in collecting duct cells.
Vesicles carrying aquaporin-2 fuse with the apical membrane, so water can follow the osmotic gradient into the salty medulla.

q: At extremely high heart rates (over about 180 beats per minute), cardiac output can actually fall. Why?
o: Diastole gets too short for the ventricles to fill
Systole becomes too short for the valves to open
The SA node runs out of its stored Ca²⁺
The atria and ventricles start contracting together
e: Faster rates shorten diastole much more than systole.
With too little filling time, end-diastolic volume and stroke volume drop enough that CO = HR × SV falls.

q: A patient with liver failure makes too little albumin and develops swelling (edema). Why?
o: Lower plasma oncotic pressure means less fluid returns to capillaries
Higher plasma oncotic pressure pulls fluid out of the capillaries into tissue
Higher arterial blood pressure forces fluid out of all vessels
Capillaries become impermeable, trapping fluid in the tissues
e: Albumin creates most of the plasma's oncotic pressure.
With less albumin, fluid stays in the tissues.

q: Which force mainly pushes fluid OUT of capillaries at the arterial end?
e: At the arterial end, hydrostatic pressure exceeds oncotic pressure, so fluid leaves.
At the venous end, oncotic pressure pulls fluid back in.

q: Which vessels carry oxygen-rich blood from the lungs to the heart?
e: The pulmonary veins return oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium.
The pulmonary arteries carry oxygen-poor blood from the right ventricle to the lungs.
t: Arteries leave the heart, veins return to it, whatever their O₂ content.

q: When a person stands up quickly, blood pools in the legs and blood pressure briefly drops. How do baroreceptors respond?
o: They fire less, increasing sympathetic drive to the heart and vessels
They fire more, increasing vagal output to slow the heart and dilate vessels
They fire less, increasing parasympathetic output to the heart
They fire more, increasing sympathetic drive to the heart and vessels
e: Baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch sense stretch.
Less stretch → less firing → the brain boosts sympathetic activity.

q: A heart beats 70 times per minute with a stroke volume of 70 mL. What is the cardiac output?
e: Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume

q: Blood leaving the left ventricle goes directly into the:
e: Left side of the heart pumps oxygenated blood to the body.
Left ventricle → aortic valve → aorta.
The right ventricle pumps into the pulmonary artery.
t: Left = body (systemic). Right = lungs (pulmonary).

q: Sickle cell disease causes painful crises in which small vessels become blocked. Using Poiseuille's law, why does blockage in small vessels so sharply reduce flow?
o: Flow depends on radius to the fourth power, so slight narrowing cuts it sharply
Flow depends mainly on vessel length, which a blockage greatly increases
Flow depends on radius to the first power, so narrowing cuts it in proportion
Flow depends on pressure squared, so blockage drops pressure sharply
e: Q ∝ r⁴: halving the radius cuts flow to 1/16.
Rigid sickled cells narrow the effective radius of tiny vessels.

q: A patient's hematocrit is 45%. What does this value measure?
o: The fraction of blood volume made up of red cells
The fraction of hemoglobin carrying oxygen
The fraction of blood volume made up of plasma
The fraction of white cells among all blood cells
e: Hematocrit is the packed red cell volume ÷ total blood volume.
45% red cells means about 55% is plasma; O₂ saturation is a different measurement.

q: The first heart sound ('lub') is mainly caused by:
o: The AV valves closing as the ventricles contract
The semilunar valves closing as the ventricles relax
The atria contracting to top off the ventricles
Blood rushing into the aorta during ejection
e: When ventricular pressure rises above atrial pressure, the mitral and tricuspid valves snap shut: S1, the start of systole.
S2 ('dub') is the aortic and pulmonary valves closing at the start of diastole.

q: Mean arterial pressure is 100 mmHg and cardiac output is 5 L min⁻¹. What is total peripheral resistance?
e: MAP = CO × TPR, so TPR = MAP ÷ CO
100 ÷ 5 = 20 mmHg·min L⁻¹

q: A ventricle has an end-diastolic volume of 120 mL and an end-systolic volume of 50 mL. What are its stroke volume and ejection fraction?
e: SV = EDV − ESV = 120 − 50 = 70 mL.
t: EF uses EDV in the denominator, not ESV.

q: Which organ produces bile?
e: The liver makes bile; the gallbladder stores and concentrates it.

q: Absorbed sugars and amino acids travel first to the liver through the:
e: The liver processes absorbed nutrients and toxins before they reach the rest of the body.

q: Shortly after a large meal, blood pH rises slightly (the 'alkaline tide'). Which explanation fits best?
o: Parietal cells send H⁺ into the stomach and HCO₃⁻ into the blood
Pancreatic bicarbonate is absorbed directly into the blood
Breathing speeds up after eating, blowing off extra CO₂
Digested amino acids act as strong bases once they reach the blood
e: Inside parietal cells, carbonic anhydrase makes H⁺ and HCO₃⁻ from CO₂ and H₂O.
H⁺ is pumped into the stomach, while HCO₃⁻ leaves the other side of the cell (in exchange for Cl⁻) and enters the blood.

q: Chief cells in the lining of the stomach secrete:
e: Chief cells release pepsinogen, the inactive precursor of pepsin.
Parietal cells make HCl and intrinsic factor; G cells make gastrin.
t: Chief = 'chief' protein digester (pepsinogen). Parietal = acid + intrinsic factor.

q: Why are pancreatic enzymes released as inactive zymogens?
o: To prevent them from digesting the pancreas itself
Because the liver must activate them
Because they work only in the stomach
e: Premature activation causes pancreatitis.

q: An infant has a thickened pyloric sphincter and vomits forcefully after every feeding. The vomit contains stomach contents but no bile. Blood tests show a high pH and high HCO₃⁻. What explains the acid–base change?
o: Loss of stomach HCl leaves extra bicarbonate in the blood
Swallowed air causes the infant to retain extra CO₂
Vomiting removes pancreatic bicarbonate from the body
The kidneys stop excreting bicarbonate after feeding
e: Each H⁺ that parietal cells secrete into the stomach leaves an HCO₃⁻ in the blood.
Normally that H⁺ is later neutralized in the duodenum; when it is vomited instead, the extra HCO₃⁻ remains, causing metabolic alkalosis.
No bile in the vomit fits a blockage before the duodenum.

q: Which structural features give the small intestine its huge absorptive surface?
e: Each level of folding multiplies the surface area.

q: Where does protein digestion begin?
e: Pepsin, activated by stomach acid, begins breaking proteins.

q: A patient with celiac disease has damaged villi in the small intestine. Which problem is expected?
o: Faster protein digestion in the mouth
e: Gluten triggers an immune attack on the intestinal lining, flattening villi and reducing surface area.

q: A drug works poorly when swallowed because it is heavily broken down before it reaches the general circulation, but it works well when dissolved under the tongue. Why?
o: Gut-absorbed drugs pass through the liver first; sublingual ones skip it
Saliva activates the drug, but stomach acid does not
The tongue absorbs drugs faster than the stomach destroys them
Under-the-tongue drugs enter the lymph and then the liver
e: Drugs absorbed from the intestine travel through the hepatic portal vein to the liver, which can metabolize much of the dose (first-pass effect).
Veins under the tongue drain into the systemic circulation, bypassing the liver on the first pass.
t: 'First-pass metabolism' is why nitroglycerin is given under the tongue.

q: G cells in the stomach release gastrin when food arrives. What is gastrin's main effect?
o: It stimulates parietal cells to secrete HCl
It stimulates the pancreas to secrete bicarbonate
It triggers the gallbladder to contract
It slows the movement of chyme into the duodenum
e: Gastrin travels in the blood and boosts acid secretion by parietal cells (directly and through histamine release).
Bicarbonate release is secretin's job; gallbladder contraction is CCK's job.

q: Salivary amylase keeps digesting starch inside a swallowed mass of food for a while. Why does it eventually stop working in the stomach?
o: Stomach acid lowers the pH and denatures it
Bile salts in the stomach coat the starch
Pepsinogen binds amylase and blocks it
Body temperature in the stomach is too high
e: Amylase works best near neutral pH (about 7).
As gastric HCl soaks into the food mass, the pH drops to about 2 and amylase denatures.

q: In clonal selection, what happens when a B cell meets the antigen its receptor matches?
o: That B cell multiplies into many plasma cells and memory cells
All B cells multiply equally, regardless of their receptor
That B cell undergoes apoptosis to prevent autoimmunity
That B cell matures into a helper T cell that secretes cytokines
e: Only the matching clone is selected and expanded.

q: In type 1 diabetes, immune cells destroy pancreatic β cells. What kind of disorder is this?
e: The immune system attacks the body's own cells, failing self-tolerance.

q: Inflammation causes redness and warmth at an injury site mainly because:
o: Histamine and other signals dilate blood vessels
Red blood cells multiply rapidly at the injury site
Damaged skin cells generate heat through metabolism
Histamine constricts vessels, trapping warm blood
e: Vasodilation brings more blood; increased permeability lets fluid and white cells enter.

q: The innate immune system:
e: Innate: skin, phagocytes, inflammation, complement.
Adaptive: B and T cells, specific and with memory.

q: Cytotoxic T cells (CD8⁺) kill:
o: Virus-infected and cancer cells showing foreign peptides on MHC I
Extracellular bacteria displaying foreign peptides on MHC II
Antigen-presenting cells displaying self peptides on MHC II
Healthy cells that have lost MHC I from their surface
e: Infected cells display viral peptides on MHC I, and CD8⁺ cells destroy them.

q: Chemotherapy drops a patient's neutrophil count very low. Which risk rises most?
e: Neutrophils are the main fast-acting phagocytes against bacteria and fungi.
With too few, even normal skin and gut microbes can cause life-threatening infection.
t: A fever in a patient with very low neutrophils is a medical emergency.

q: After strep throat, a child develops heart valve damage because antibodies against a strep protein also bind heart tissue. This is an example of:
o: Immunodeficiency from too few B cells
e: The strep protein resembles a heart protein, so antibodies made against the microbe cross-react with self.
This is how rheumatic fever damages heart valves.

q: HIV infects and destroys mainly which cells?
e: HIV binds CD4.
Losing helper T cells cripples both antibody and cytotoxic responses (AIDS).

q: MHC class I molecules present which peptides, and on which cells?
o: Cytosolic peptides, on nearly all nucleated cells
Peptides from engulfed microbes, only on APCs
Peptides from inside the cell, only on red blood cells
Whole antigens from outside, only on B cells
e: MHC I displays fragments of proteins made inside the cell, so a virus-infected cell shows viral peptides to CD8⁺ T cells.
Almost every nucleated cell has MHC I; mature red cells, which lack nuclei, do not.
t: Rule of 8: MHC I × CD8 = 8 and MHC II × CD4 = 8.

q: Heating a protein destroys its 3-D shape. Antibodies against the native protein no longer bind it, but T cells specific for the protein still respond. Why?
o: T cells see processed peptide fragments, not 3-D shape
T cells bind only to sugars attached to the protein
Antibodies recognize only short linear sequences
Heating raises MHC expression only on B cells
e: Many antibodies bind conformational epitopes, which unfolding destroys.
T cells recognize short peptides cut from the protein and shown on MHC, so unfolding doesn't change what they see.

q: Which immune cells differentiate into antibody-secreting plasma cells?
e: Activated B cells can differentiate into plasma cells that secrete antibodies.

q: Helper T cells (CD4⁺) recognize antigen presented on:
e: MHC II is found on antigen-presenting cells (macrophages, dendritic cells, B cells).
CD8⁺ cytotoxic T cells recognize MHC I, found on all nucleated cells.
t: Rule of 8: CD4 × MHC II = 8; CD8 × MHC I = 8.

q: Which type of muscle forms the walls of blood vessels and the digestive tract?
e: Smooth muscle is involuntary and non-striated.
It lines hollow organs such as blood vessels, the gut, the bladder and the uterus.

q: T-tubules in muscle fibers:
o: Carry action potentials deep into the fiber to trigger Ca²⁺ release
Store Ca²⁺ and release it into the cytosol when stimulated
Connect the fiber to tendon so force reaches the bone
Link neighboring fibers electrically so they contract as a single unit
e: T-tubules let the signal reach the sarcoplasmic reticulum throughout the fiber at once.

q: People with darker skin living at high latitudes are at higher risk of vitamin D deficiency in winter. Which explanation fits best?
o: More melanin absorbs the UVB needed to make vitamin D
More melanin breaks down the vitamin D the skin makes
Darker skin has fewer cells containing cholesterol
Cold air blocks the skin from absorbing any light
e: Skin makes vitamin D when UVB converts 7-dehydrocholesterol.
Melanin absorbs UVB; where winter sunlight is weak, less UVB reaches that precursor, so less vitamin D is made.

q: Why do long bones in children grow in length but adult bones do not?
o: Children's growth plates are still active cartilage; adults' have fused
Adults have no osteoblasts, so new bone matrix can't be laid down
Children's bones lack calcium, so they lengthen under mechanical load
Adults completely stop secreting growth hormone after puberty
e: Cartilage at the growth plates divides and is replaced by bone.
After puberty, the plates close (ossify).

q: What is the basic contractile unit of a skeletal muscle fiber?
e: Sarcomeres are arranged end to end, from Z-line to Z-line.

q: Which layer of the skin contains blood vessels, sweat glands and hair follicles?
e: The dermis is the connective-tissue layer under the epidermis, with vessels, nerves, glands and follicles.
The epidermis (including the stratum corneum and stratum basale) has no blood vessels.

q: A patient with a parathyroid tumor makes too much PTH. She has bone pain and develops kidney stones. Which explanation links these findings?
o: Bone resorption raises blood Ca²⁺, so more Ca²⁺ reaches the urine
Calcium is deposited in bone, so the kidney traps the excess
PTH blocks the kidney from filtering any Ca²⁺
Low blood Ca²⁺ causes bone pain and stone formation
e: Excess PTH drives osteoclasts to resorb bone (causing pain) and raises blood Ca²⁺.
Although PTH boosts Ca²⁺ reabsorption, so much Ca²⁺ is filtered that urine Ca²⁺ rises and can form stones.
t: Classic hyperparathyroidism: 'bones, stones, groans and moans'.

q: In a resting skeletal muscle fiber, what prevents myosin heads from binding to actin?
o: Tropomyosin covers the myosin-binding sites on actin
Troponin is bound tightly to the myosin heads
Titin holds the thick filaments away from actin
Calmodulin keeps all the myosin heads in a locked state
e: Tropomyosin strands lie along the thin filament, blocking myosin-binding sites.
When Ca²⁺ binds troponin, troponin pulls tropomyosin aside and cross-bridges can form.

q: A person picks up a light cup and then a heavy grocery bag with the same arm. How does the biceps produce the extra force for the bag?
o: By recruiting more motor units and firing them faster
By making each fiber contract partly, then fully
By converting slow-twitch fibers into fast-twitch fibers
By lengthening each sarcomere before it contracts
e: A single fiber contracts all-or-none, so force is graded by how many motor units are active (recruitment).
Firing each unit faster also adds force through summation.

q: Which mineral makes up most of bone's hard matrix?
e: Hydroxyapatite gives hardness; collagen gives flexibility.

q: Osteoclast activity increases when blood calcium is low. Which hormone drives this?
e: PTH indirectly activates osteoclasts to release calcium from bone.

q: Which protein forms the thick filaments of a sarcomere?
e: Thick filaments: myosin. Thin filaments: actin with troponin and tropomyosin.

q: In the neuron diagram, where are voltage-gated Na⁺ channels most concentrated in this myelinated axon?
e: 4 marks a node of Ranvier, the gap between myelin segments.
Action potentials regenerate only at the nodes (saltatory conduction).

q: Two unaffected parents have both an affected son and an affected daughter (shown). What is the most likely mode of inheritance?
e: Unaffected parents with affected children → recessive.
An affected daughter of an unaffected father rules out X-linked recessive.
